Has the Unemployment Insurance Act been studied, since January 1, 1954, by the government or by any officials thereof, to determine whether provision should be made for a person who has qualified for unemployment insurance benefits to continue receiving such benefits until such person is re-employed?

DENTIFRICE ADVERTISEMENTS Mr. Knowles:
1.	Has the Department of National Health and Welfare made any investigation or examination of tooth pastes, tooth powders or other dentifrices being sold in Canada, to determine whether or not such products measure up to the claims made for them in advertisements appearing on their behalf?
2.	If so, what are the results of such investigation or examination?
3.	Have any dentifrice advertisements been found to be misleading? If so, in what way?
4.	Have any dentifrice advertisements been found to offend against the provisions of the Food and Drugs Act, as assented to on May 14, 1953? If so, in what way?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
1.	Yes. Tooth pastes and tooth powders have been analysed in the laboratories of the food and drug divisions during the past few years. Manufacturers have also been requested to submit data in support of claims made or proposed for advertising purposes.
2.	The results of the analysis revealed no violation of the Food and Drugs Act or regulations. Some of the data submitted was not considered adequate to support the advertised claims and manufacturers have withdrawn such claims voluntarily.
3.	Yes. Some dentifrice advertisements have been found misleading in that statements were made that could not be supported by adequate evidence.
4.	The Food and Drugs Act, as assented to on May 14, 1953, has not yet been proclaimed; therefore no offence can be committed at this time in contravention of the revised act.
5.	One dental association asked for the department's views on anti-enzymes as related to dental health and the advertising of such products.
6.	The dental association was informed that manufacturers were requested to submit clinical evidence in support of their claims and where such evidence was not scientifically acceptable, they were asked to withdraw such claims.
7.	The Department of National Health and Welfare is not aware that the American Dental Association has ever advertised a dentifrice.
8.	See answer to No. 7 above.

speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Will the Prime Minister inform the house if it is on the instructions of the government that the Canadian representatives at Geneva are not attending the discussions on Indo-China?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, it is not on instructions of the government. It is no doubt as a consequence of the discussions [DOT]we had about the matter before the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) left for that conference. As I stated the other day, our position was that we were not committed to the actions that are proceeding in Indo-China and had no standing to ask to participate in the decisions that might be arrived at in respect of that situation; we wanted to be careful and not depart in any way from the attitude we have maintained in the house that our commitments with respect to action in the East were limited to those that were under the aegis of the United Nations, and that if it became

On the orders of the day:

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I have two questions to ask the Prime Minister, of which I have given him notice. The first is this: Was the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) expressing government policy when he said in Edmonton on April 28, as reported in a Canadian Press dispatch in the Globe and Mail of April 29, that "there will be little, if any, change in taxes for years to come."

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I assume that the hon. member is referring to the report in the Globe and Mail of April 29 as the basis for this question. I have secured the report and I find that nowhere in it is the minister reported as having said the words used in the hon. gentleman's question. As a matter of fact, the report states:
He told the Canadian Club that despite existence of the hydrogen and atomic bombs, the need for conventional weapons is just as great.
Then there are some words that are indicated as a quotation which are as follows:
The H-bomb has not lessened the magnitude of the defence operation. There is still a need for a navy, army and air force of about the present size as the minimum force necessary to enable us to do our job.
Then the reporter goes on to say:
Observers said this was a clear indication that defence budgets will remain at the present level for years-around $2 billion annually. Defence forms at least 40 per cent of the national budget. Thus tax reductions, if any, would necessarily have to be small.
It seems to have been the impression made upon those who heard the speech that there

was not likely to be a change in taxes for years to come. There seems to have been no such statement made by the minister, and it may or may not be an accurate conclusion to draw from the statement of the minister that the situation seemed to require the maintenance of as large forces as we have at the present time. In any event there has been no government policy determined with respect to taxes for future years, and there will be no determination until we know just exactly what is the situation we have to budget for in those future years.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
As I think my question indicated, I was quoting from the dispatch. I should like to read the words again and ask the Prime Minister if he thinks what he has said indicates any inaccuracy in the sense of this dispatch. 1 read the words:
Defence Minister Claxton indicated today that there will be little change in taxes, if any, for years to come.
As I understood the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) he said nothing to differ substantially from that.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
The reporter says that
the minister indicated that there would be no change in taxes for years to come. Then he goes on to explain how that indication was made. It was made by the statement that under present conditions it appeared necessary to maintain the strength of the forces now in existence.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I do not like to be inaccurate, so again I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he thinks there is any inaccuracy in the statement which I have read?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: There is only this inaccuracy. The statement appears to have been a conclusion drawn by the reporter. From the statement that the forces will have to remain at their present strength he draws a conclusion about the taxes, and whether or not that is an accurate conclusion to draw from the statement is a matter of opinion.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
On behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs I should like to make a statement concerning disarmament. In its resolution on disarmament of November 28 last, the United Nations general assembly suggested that the disarmament commission study the desirability of establishing a subcommittee which should seek in private an acceptable solution of the disarmament problem and report to the commission as soon as possible. The commission has now set up a subcommittee on which Canada is represented together with France, the United Kingdom, the United States and the Soviet union.
The establishment of the subcommittee is considered by the Canadian government as an important step towards the settlement of a vital problem, the importance of which has been underlined by recent developments in the field of atomic and hydrogen weapons. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) will be the Canadian representative on the subcommittee which will begin private talks on or about May 13 in London. Mr. N. A. Robertson, Canadian High Commissioner in the United Kingdom and Mr. David M. Johnson, Canadian permanent


representative to the United Nations, will be alternate representatives in London and in New York respectively.
The disarmament commission has recommended that the subcommittee submit a report of its discussions not later than July 15 next. The commission itself is called upon to report to the general assembly and the security council not later than September 1, 1954. The Canadian government earnestly hopes that these renewed efforts on the part of the United Nations will result in substantial progress being achieved in finding a solution to the problem of disarmament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO EXTENSION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I propose to make a statement tomorrow about the further legislation to be introduced. However I can assure my hon. friend at the present time we have come to the conclusion we will not at this session ask parliament to extend the Emergency Powers Act. We felt it was a grave decision to make because there is still a pretty explosive situation existing in the world. I hope the situation will not require the exercise of any but normal powers by the governor in council. But should it develop that there would have to be, in the interests of the safety of the nation, powers exercised that are not normally conferred upon the governor in council by existing legislation, we would have to resort to the War Measures Act. I sincerely hope that will never be necessary while I am a member of the government.

I do not want to hedge on these words. If my predecessor, or any of my colleagues, speaking on their responsibilities as members of the cabinet, have said that we will participate in the cost of building the Marpole bridge, then we will honour the commitment.

I have also found further corroboration of the fact that commitments were made. For example, on April 15 of this year, during the Easter recess, the minister of public works in British Columbia was quoted as follows in the Vancouver Province:
Mr. Gaglardi insisted the Right Hon. C. D. Howe had made a commitment to help B.C., and said, "I still believe the government will stick by its previous promises. I still refuse to accept anything but a positive answer."
And then he added this paragraph:
"Mr. Winters is a very fine man and I'm sure he'll help."

It is a statement
of fact.

reference to a statement made in the B.C. legislature by Mr. Gaglardi. The article says:
Before the last legislative session Mr. Gaglardi visited Ottawa and reported he had a pledge of help from Rt. Hon. C. D. Howe.

-Defence Production Minister C. D. Howe had told him in writing that the federal government was "not interested at this time in any more than a payment of $400,000 toward the Marpole crossing."

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
May I say a word, since my past remarks have been quoted by my hon. friend? This discussion of a bridge across the north arm of the Fraser river has been continuing for a good many years. In the beginning it was a fairly simple proposal of replacing the present swing bridge by a lift bridge at or near the same location. Conditions were different at that time in that we were operating the Sea Island airport. Discussions were held, but never with any agreement between the city and the province. I had said that if the city and the province were able to come forward with a scheme in which they both agreed, the federal government might be expected to contribute something up to one-third of the cost. Remember this was an indication given a good many years ago. Well, the city and the province never did agree, and they have not agreed to this date. But the province went up into the stratosphere and talked about a $7 million or $8 million bridge, which incidentally might give a better access to the airport but was really intended as another artery to the international border. At that time I indicated that we were not interested in a bridge for that purpose, that there is no federal responsibility for such a structure built wholly within a province. I still say, and I have repeated more recently, that if the bridge is confined to replacing the present bridge and serves no other purpose, and if the city and the province agreed on such a proposal, and agreed on their participation, the federal government would consider assistance.
That is the extent of my undertaking at any time. If the $400,000 figure was mentioned it then represented about one-third of the total expenditure that we were discussing; but I may say that much water has gone over the dam since then, and I consider that the present Minister of Public Works is not bound in any way by discussions about a totally different project which took place seven or eight years ago.

I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether the government is prepared now to make a contribution to a bridge over the north arm of the Fraser. There is no doubt at all-and I am sure he
Supply-Public Works
will agree with me-that there has to be some change made either in the present bridge or there has to be a new bridge built. Frankly I think it would be foolish simply to build up the old bridge. It is an old wooden structure, over fifty years old. This airport is certainly one of the two leading airports in Canada. The air force base on Sea island, which is part of the airport, is vital to the defence of the west coast, and it would be poor business not to build a proper bridge when a bridge is being built. Is the government prepared to pay one-third of the cost of such bridge? If it is not prepared to pay the one-third, approximately what contribution would it make? The provincial government has gone ahead and prepared plans.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Of what?
Of a bridge which is to be known as the Oak street bridge. It is a short distance-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is a high level bridge leading to the international boundary.

It is a high level bridge, yes; that is right. But a bridge to the airport should be a high level bridge; it should not be opened for every little scow that comes down with a load of sawdust. That is what is happening now. It is being opened hundreds of times a year. A businesslike approach to the question would be for the dominion to come off its high horse of not being willing to make any payment at all and agree to pay one-third of the cost of the plan, provided that plan is approved by the Department of Public Works. I think Vancouver is unanimous on this question. I would be surprised if any of the hon. members from greater Vancouver differed from the stand that I have taken. Of course they will have to speak for themselves, but this is a very serious matter. Any change in the bridge has been held up for many years.
As I said on April 9, such a condition would not have been allowed to exist in central Canada for six months simply because the seat of government is here in central Canada. Because we are 2,400 miles or 2,500 miles away it seems to be easy for the powers that be to shrug their shoulders and find someone else to blame. As a result nothing has been done. I hope that that position is not going to be taken on this question today.

speechtext:
