a bridge leading to the airport only. That is all we are interested in. The city and the province have never at any time in my experience, in my nineteen years in this house, agreed on any proposal to build a bridge to serve the airport. My hon. friend is talking of a hypothetical bridge. There are bridges and bridges. Some we might be inclined to help out and others we would not help out. There is no obligation whatever on the federal government to assist in financing any bridge. It is a bridge within a province and a bridge within two municipalities.
A great many access roads have been built to airports without any federal help. I cannot think at the moment where we have helped access to any airport except in the case of Victoria. In that instance, there was an insistent demand that we build a civilian airport closer to town, and after a good deal of discussion and negotiation it was decided by the province and by ourselves that we could both save money by improving the access to the existing military airport, which was done. I cannot think of another case in the whole history of airports where the government has made a substantial contribution to providing access from a town to an airport. That is the position. I think the position today is that if the city and the province were to agree on a bridge solely for the purpose of giving access to the Sea Island airport and wanted to bring it along and sit down with us I do not think that contribution is barred, but certainly there is no definite commitment for a contribution as far as my discussions are concerned.
Does the minister mean that the dominion government will make no contribution whatever unless this bridge is to be one solely to serve the airport?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is correct, so far as I am concerned.

May I say that that is a ridiculous stand to take. If it is good business to ouild a high-level bridge a few hundred yards further up the river, even though that oridge serves a further purpose and will help with regard to traffic to the airport, surely a contribution should be made to that bridge. Why should the government take the position that it will not contribute one cent unless a bridge is built which serves only the airport? The Minister of Trade and Commerce is a good businessman, one of the best in Canada. I am amazed that he would take a position of that kind. I think that on reflection he will not stand by that statement. He will realize, just as must everyone in this house, that if it is more practical to build in


another spot a bridge which can serve more than the one purpose-that is, more than the airport-then that is what should be done and the dominion contribution should go into that bridge.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we were talking about past commitments. The Minister of Public Works will speak about what we will do today or tomorrow. I am talking about past commitments. I made clear to Mr. Carson the stand I have taken. I made it clear to all concerned. I have been referring to past commitments that had been made by myself. My hon. friend was referring to commitments made by myself. What the government will do under present-day conditions is something that the Minister of Public Works will deal with.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce admits that he did make commitments at least to the extent of $400,000 for help in the construction of the bridge?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The amount of $400,000 was not mentioned but a certain definite proposal had been put forward by the province and a somewhat similar one by the city. I said that if they would build the bridge as planned, which was a lift bridge, providing reasonable freedom from interruption to the traffic to the airport, I thought the government might contribute up to one-third.

Mr. Chairman, there is one thing that is quite definite in all this discussion and that is that a bridge is needed across the north arm of the Fraser river. I drove a milk wagon over that bridge forty-five years ago and at that time there was a sign there which said not to trot your horses. It has not improved a great deal during the intervening time. It seems to me that the initiative for the building of the bridge rests with the provincial government. When the provincial government has decided on building a bridge, I believe that this government has a responsibility in connection with a contribution, although I cannot agree with the minister that a bridge would be built there solely .for the airport. You cannot build a bridge there just solely for the airport. But a bridge built there as a bridge for general traffic would undoubtedly help traffic to and from the airport.
I think it was the Vancouver Sun which put on a little demonstration the last time the Prime Minister was in Vancouver just to show how easy it was to hold up traffic going to the airport on that bridge. But at any time that definite plans are made for building a bridge-and I say again that matter rests with the provincial government and not with the city of Vancouver or the federal

government-and when those plans are there, I will be ready to urge the federal government to make a contribution.
I believe that the contribution will have to be more than $400,000. The most recent figure that I saw-I would not be too definite now as to what it was-was, I think, several million dollars. A $400,000 contribution is neither here nor there. As the minister was heard to say one other time "What's a million dollars anyway?" I say again that I shall be glad to add my words and efforts to those of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra to get a bridge that is badly needed there; but I believe that the initiative should come from the provincial government.

Perhaps I might just state what the position is since we last discussed the matter on April 9 here in committee. Since that time I have been reviewing the files to see what has been the nature of these alleged commitments. From the files I have found that they are mostly newspaper reports. Just what more there is to it, I do not know.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has said today that there was a commitment.

I was going to add that when my hon. friend interrupted. In the meantime the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said before the committee that he promised some time ago that the federal government would participate in building a low-level bridge whose primary purpose was to provide access to the airport. I might state also that Hon. P. A. Gaglardi was here this week and saw me on Tuesday, at which time we discussed the bridge. He then talked in terms of a high-level bridge costing in excess of what he estimated to be $10 million. I told him I was surprised at this high-level bridge proposal. He said it had been before the department for some time, but in fact I was not aware of it. I still thought our discussion related to a low-level bridge which was estimated to cost about $1,200,000, and that is how the $400,000 figure arose. I told Mr. Gaglardi that in the light of all these developments I was perfectly prepared to review the whole subject, to discuss it further with my colleagues and then to let him know what the decision would be.

As a Vancouver member I have an interest in the construction of bridges which is equal to that of my friends the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. I do not think that this is the time that we should muddy the waters in connection with this discussion. It seems to me that in the
Supply-Public Works
minds of different people we are putting the cart before the horse. My good friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has spoken of a crossing over the north arm of the Fraser river. I think that what we must realize first and foremost is that a crossing might mean a crossing at Marpole or a crossing at the southern end of Oak street. There is no doubt that what has been said by my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway is quite true, namely that 45 years ago the Marpole bridge was then fairly new and that at that time it was necessary not to exceed the speed limit by trotting your horses. Since that time there has been no improvement in the Marpole situation but rather a great deterioration by virtue of age.
I think we have to look upon this thing in the light of the traffic conditions today. First of all, if we start talking about Marpole high suspension, we are running into a deadend street for the simple reason that it would be a detriment to navigation by virtue of its close location to the airport. I am not trying to bring up a question between the bascule bridge that is a possibility or a high-level suspension bridge, but the Marpole bridge as now located is very close to the landing field of the international airport in Vancouver. Consequently I think it would be poor business to consider in that particular area a high-level suspension bridge. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra spoke about a crossing over the north arm of the Fraser river. A crossing might mean a crossing at Marpole or it might mean a crossing at the end of Oak street. When you get into the question of $8 million or $10 million bridge construction, you are certainly going to have a high-level suspension bridge.
Whether a crossing is to be decided upon at this time I am not prepared to say for the simple reason that it is my considered opinion that before any definite and specific action can be taken, either by the municipal or provincial government of British Columbia, or the federal government here, the first thing to be done is to ascertain who is going to own the international airport. When we have that question settled it is quite possible that one or other of the potential crossings over the north arm of the Fraser river will have automatically eliminated itself.
Last summer and fall there was an editorial in the Vancouver Sun with respect to the Marpole bridge based upon the possibility of handling the project in three ways. The municipality of Richmond would construct the southern approach, the city of Vancouver construct the northern approach, with the provincial government possibly sharing the construction of the central span.

Supply-Public Works
That, to me, is very sound; but just the same is the potential crossing of the Fraser going to be at Marpole, or is it going to be the southern extension of the Oak street bridge? I do not think I can quite go along with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra on this question at this time because on the basis of his approach I think we are going to make confusion all the more confounded, and heaven knows we have enough of that now.
It seems to me that the logical thing to do now is to ascertain at the earliest possible moment whether the federal government and the municipalities can come to an agreement on the sale of the international airport. When we have done that we will then be in a much better position to judge whether the crossing to be established is going to be at Marpole or at the southern end of Oak street.
In this whole question, Mr. Chairman, there can be no doubt that we have more to consider than simply the problem of traffic in a city which is growing at the terrific rate at which Vancouver is now growing. There is much more to this problem than that of a mere traffic bottleneck. In the event of our having to evacuate the city of Vancouver we are in a positively untenable position at the present time. We do not know, nor can anyone in this house know, regardless of how well informed they may be with respect to foreign affairs, when some trigger-happy character may pull the string, and if that should occur the city of Vancouver, as I have said, is in a very bad position. I believe the aspect of possible evacuation should be considered in connection with bridge outlets from the metropolitan area of Vancouver.
I am no authority on this aspect but it seems to me that we would be well advised to discuss a crossing over the Fraser when we have first decided what is going to happen to the international airport. When that is decided then one or other of the crossings now in people's minds will automatically eliminate itself and the various governments concerned, municipal, provincial, and federal, will be in a much sounder position to come to an agreement if for no other reason than that the expediency of potential evacuation might bring about an agreement satisfactory to all concerned.
I am just as anxious as the two hon. members from Vancouver who have already spoken on this question that we have an adequate crossing over the Fraser river, but I believe that before we come to any final decision as to where that crossing is going to be it is essential that the government of British Columbia, and the municipalities of

Vancouver and Richmond, know exactly what the score is with respect to the ownership of the international airport. In this instance, Mr. Chairman, I believe we could possibly hasten the construction of adequate crossings over the Fraser river if we do not now rush into it until such time as we know where that crossing is actually going to be located.

Mr. Chairman, earlier this week I spoke on this question in this house and today my name has been brought into the discussion in regard to certain correspondence between the Minister of Trade and Commerce and myself. At that time the Minister of Trade and Commerce-and I think this was in 1951-made his suggestion of financial assistance being conditional upon the city of Vancouver and the provincial government becoming interested in this bridge. Whether a mistaken report was issued in that regard is not my responsibility but in numerous speeches I mentioned the amount of $400,000. I also mentioned the fact that this was a provisional amount.
We are talking about a bridge which is 65 years old and which during October 1953 opened no less than 664 times. I represent people who are deeply concerned with this matter and I can say that my people in Richmond believe that the federal government have a responsibility if the airport is purchased by the federal government. I said that earlier this week and I say it again.
In regard to a southern highway from Vancouver to the United States, there is confirmation of that in the brief which the provincial government of British Columbia brought to Ottawa some time last year. If hon. members read that brief they will find no mention of a Marpole bridge. There is mention of a highway to the United States. If it is the opinion of the provincial government of British Columbia that this bridge is being built only to supplement a highway to the United States then I would doubt that the federal government had any financial responsibility. But in my speech on Tuesday I outlined certain specifications in regard to my support of one-third of the financial cost, and if I remember correctly this is what I said: that plans and specifications be made and offered by the provincial government of my province to the Minister of Public Works so he may then know what these plans are. It has been stated in the Vancouver press that these plans are already here, but I do not believe that is true. I believe I can place the responsibility for that statement upon a provincial cabinet minister who gave it to the Vancouver press. I understand the final

plans have yet to be decided upon and I have some doubt they have been drawn at this moment.
However, when we start talking about federal responsibility then I cannot but agree with my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. If we do purchase the airport at a cost of $1,100,000-I think that is the amount suggested-then I hope the Minister of Public Works will take a look at this plan in regard to the Oak street bridge. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard made some suggestion that an offer had been made to Richmond to build the southern approach to the bridge, but I think he was in error. The municipality of Richmond has not the money and the suggestion has not been made to them that they build that southern approach. What was suggested some time ago was that the city of Vancouver would build the northern end of the bridge, the federal government the southern end of the bridge and the provincial government the main span. I do not think that the suggestion was offered very seriously but it was offered late last year.
There is no doubt in my mind that the municipality of Richmond needs a crossing. It is quite clear to me that the crossing is going to be at Oak street because the provincial government has already bought large quantities of land in my municipality- title to which I understand has been given to either the province or one of their officials. I happen to know the people who sold the property to them, and I think you can take it that, as I said on Tuesday, the intentions of the provincial government of British Columbia are sincere. The engineers have told the provincial government that a high-level bridge at Oak street is quite permissible having regard to the act that governs the control of airways. The engineers in British Columbia seem to be of the opinion that this would be no detriment to the landing of aircraft.
I said last year at several meetings on the coast that it was my opinion that at this time the present Marpole span should be done away with and that a new span should be built 30 feet above high water level which would allow every vessel using the north arm, except one, to go under the bridge without any suspension of traffic. I understand that one dredge that goes to New Westminster once a week would have to have the bridge raised for it, but that is all. As I said last Tuesday, the bridge was opened 664 times in a month. This is a disgrace for which responsibility should not be attributed to the federal government but to
Supply-Public Works
the provincial government of British Columbia because there is no doubt that at this time there is a contract signed by the municipality of Richmond and the provincial government whereby the provincial government accepts full responsibility for that bridge. I have seen the document. It is in the hands of the municipality of Richmond, and I am quite sure if the Minister of Public Works wishes it I can get him a copy.
I think every member from British Columbia is sincere about this matter, and I hope the people at home are not being kidded too much with respect to this bridge. On any street in Vancouver, Burnaby or Richmond you will find a different rumour regarding what the federal government proposes to do. The truth should be put on the record, and as one who is vitally interested I may say that as far as I know I do not think the federal government have moved on this matter. I would suggest to the Minister of Public Works, as I did on Tuesday, that they do not move until plans and specifications are in their hands showing a sincere intention on the part of the provincial government to build the bridge.

I want to say a word about the bridge, one end of which happens to be in my own constituency. I will assure the committee now that it is going to be just a word because it seems to me it is quite superfluous for us to talk at too great length about the details of who is going to pay for how much until we have some exact, hard and concrete proposition in front of us. I for one was very glad to hear the assurances of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Public Works that when the authorities primarily responsible for building the bridge, the provincial government of British Columbia, come to the federal government with a hard and fast proposition this government will be prepared to give it fair consideration. As far as I am concerned, at this moment that is good enough for me.
I want to make one or two observations on the question of principle. It would be very presumptuous for me, as a new member of the house, to say to what degree the national authority should step in so far as the question of bridges is concerned, but as I read the constitution of Canada I see no obligation whatever upon the government of Canada to pay for any bridges except on three different scores, if bridges are interprovincial, if they are international or if they are, for some peculiar reason, required for primarily national purposes.
There are three national purposes which might be involved with respect to the Marpole bridge. In the first place, if the federal
423S

Supply-Public Works authority does acquire the airport at Vancouver, which I certainly hope comes to pass because I believe the offer now made is a fair one, then it seems to me only common sense that the government of Canada will require access to their airport because it is no good unless you have access to it and access away from it. Just before coming here for this session I made a speech at the air force base on Sea island and my audience literally galloped out on me at about a quarter to five because they wanted to get to the Marpole bridge to beat the traffic. Otherwise they would be held up for about two hours. There, of course, is a very practical reason why we need a proper bridge to get to one of the most vital airports in the whole Dominion of Canada.
The second consideration about which I would remind the committee is of course the question of navigation in its relation to traffic. Just the other day we heard the Minister of Public Works tell how fairly the government has dealt with the province of Ontario with respect to the bridge over the canal at Burlington, Ontario. I am not saying this is the case, but if the same considerations apply in respect of traffic over the Fraser river as apply in respect of traffic over the canal at Burlington, namely, that it is an advantageous thing to build a certain type of bridge in order to facilitate navigation, a federal responsibility, then it seems to me that the federal authority would be prepared to give sympathetic consideration to any hard and concrete proposition that is made. I may have a bit more to say if a hard and concrete proposition is ever placed before the federal authority, but all I want to say now is that I am delighted with the assurances we have received this afternoon from the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Public Works that when the federal government have something real to go on they will give it proper consideration.

Before we drop this subject I should like to have the minister make perfectly clear exactly what the position of the government is to be on this bridge. On April 9, as found at page 3940 of Hansard, he said:
We have, to date, told the government of British Columbia that there is no federal government responsibility with respect to the bridge, and that we cannot participate in the cost.
Today there has been some change in the attitude of the government. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has admitted that he at least made a commitment several years ago, and the Minister of Public Works has said he will have another look at the question. That does not go very far. I should like to know exactly what the government stand is
[Mr. Philpott.l

to be. Is the government now prepared to participate in the cost of a bridge over the north arm of the Fraser river and, if so, under what conditions and to what extent?

My position is exactly the same as it was. As we have just heard, a bridge of this type is not normally a federal government responsibility. It was for that reason we told the government of British Columbia that under normal circumstances this was not our responsibility and we did not see that we could participate. Then hon. members brought to my attention the fact that certain of my colleagues were alleged to have made commitments with respect to the bridge. My hon. friend heard today the extent to which the Minister of Trade and Commerce said he had told the government of British Columbia the federal government was prepared to participate. In the light of that, only this week I told the minister of public works of British Columbia that I was quite prepared to review the whole case having regard to all these considerations. I was thinking in terms of a low level bridge. He apparently is thinking in terms of a high level bridge.
As other hon. members have said here today, I want to see his clear-cut proposals. I should like to know something about the extent to which the city is prepared to participate. The minister from British Columbia told me this week he was not able to inform me of the extent to which the city would share. He had no agreement with them. There are details to be worked out, and I am not in a position to tell the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, much as I should like to oblige him, specifically on what basis and to what extent the federal government is prepared to participate. That is a matter that must be studied fully in the light of the facts that are still to be placed before us.
Can we take it from the minister's statement that the dominion government is prepared to participate in the construction of the new bridge?
I must have the facts before I can give any such assurance.
The minister is not making any commitment whatever today that the government will participate in the construction of the new bridge?

I am making no commitment beyond an undertaking to restudy this whole matter. While I say that, I have in mind the position taken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce today, and -hon. members may be assured that will not be overlooked.

I should like to deal with the item for a public building in Vernon, B.C. I was rather surprised to see that the amount had been dropped from $100,000 to $25,000 and so far as I am aware no reason has been given to the city of Vernon, the board of trade or any of the interested parties. I was rather surprised because it indicates a change of policy on the part of the new minister.
The history of this public building goes back four or five years. Some years ago a new site was acquired by the government for this building and about three years ago the government informed the city of Vernon that plans were started for this building. It was hoped tenders would be called that fall. Two years ago the present Minister of Fisheries was in Vernon, was taken over the site, and definitely promised on his return he would see that something was done to speed up this work. A previous minister, Mr. Mayhew, also promised the same thing to the city of Vernon.
The previous minister of public works made a definite promise that this building had a high priority and would be started and completed last year, 1953. I have a whole file of letters if the minister wishes to see them to corroborate what I am saying. The last one is dated February 4, 1953. The assistant district architect for the Department of Public Works in Vancouver told the city of Vernon that it was the federal government's intention to commence construction of the new post office in Vernon immediately. The city wrote saying they were naturally very pleased and were looking forward to the completion of the public building before the year was out.
The Minister of Fisheries stated, after inspecting the site of the new federal building and thoroughly examining the plans, the present inadequate post office and the plans for its use as a city hall, that upon his return to Ottawa he would take up the matter with the Minister of Public Works in an effort to have construction expedited. That was January 20, 1952. I have a letter from-

I think I can save considerable time for the committee if the hon. member will let me state what the position is. We propose to construct a building in Vernon. We are waiting now for certain other departments of government to decide whether or not they wish space in that building. We expect those decisions will be finalized later this year and we aim at having the plans ready next year.

I thank the minister for his reply, but I had the same reply nearly two years ago. A form was sent around to each
Supply-Public Works
department asking what space they required in the new building, and it was a question of having those forms completed about a year and a half ago.

Mr. Chairman, I do not really see that this is getting us anywhere. I just told the hon. member what the position is. It seems to me the practice is growing of quoting everybody except the minister responsible for the department. I have told the hon. member what the position is. I hope he will take my word for that.

I should like to give the minister a change by conveying to him the appreciation of my constituents at the announcement that a new post office is to be built in Nanaimo. I should like also to question him as to the policy of his department in releasing such news. At Easter, before I left for my constituency, the minister was kind enough to send me a letter informing me the department was not going to build a breakwater at Cowichan bay. This sad news I had to convey to my constituents. The first thing that confronted me when I landed in Nanaimo was a report in the local paper that the president of the local Liberal association announced that a contract had been let for a new post office in Nanaimo.
I am given to understand that the Minister of Public Works is not responsible for such disclosures but it is the work, shall we say, of one of his colleagues who is delegated to take a paternal interest in the province from which he comes. I should like to say this is really a very bad policy. I am quite sure the minister does not need any information from me to know just what little pile of hay I made out of that particular situation at the three meetings I addressed at Nanaimo during the Easter recess.

I wish to convey my appreciation to the minister and to his department for the proposed erection of a new post office in the town of Cloverdale. I understand tenders have been called for the demolition of the city hall building in the city of New Westminster. So far as we can gather, this is supposed to be the site of a new federal building in the city of New Westminster. I have just a few pertinent questions with reference to both the Cloverdale area and New Westminster. What branches of the various departments are going to be housed in the particular buildings, and can any information be given as to the size of the proposed building in New Westminster? Is it contemplated that it shall be erected later this year?

As the hon. member said, we have called for tenders for the demolition of the present buildings on the site acquired.

Supply-Public Works
We are in the process now of preparing plans for a building to house the post office, customs, unemployment insurance commission and soldier settlement, as well as perhaps some other departments of government. We have not assembled all the information, and the plans are only now in the state of preparation by the department.
What is it intended to house in the Cloverdale federal building?
So far as I can determine, from information at hand, that building is for postal purposes. The contract was awarded to the Allan and Viner Construction Company, in the amount of $135,290.

Item agreed to.
Acquisition, construction and improvements of public buildings-
375.	Yukon and Northwest Territories, $670,000.

When does the minister
expect work will be completed on the new federal building in Whitehorse, and when will it be ready for occupancy?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: See the president of your local Liberal association.

If the hon. member for
Yukon outsmarts the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on one or two occasions he should not take it too badly. As of March-and that is the latest figure I have-the building at Whitehorse was 85 per cent completed. It should be finished this fall.
What provision has been made for water and sewer services?
For water there will be a well; for sewage there will be septic tanks until the water system in Whitehorse is completed.

Item agreed to.
Acquisition, construction and improvements of public buildings-
376.	Unforeseen improvements, $1,200,000.
Does this item include any specific amounts, or is it in the nature of a reserve fund to cover emergency situations?

It is to cover items now
unforeseen, and is in the nature of a reserve fund.

I would draw to the minister's attention the post office building at Woodstock, Ontario. A few years ago some satisfactory alterations were made to this building, which had the effect of improving the facilities offered. However the entrance and exit leave much to be desired. To get into the building one has to climb two or three steps, and immediately he is confronted with an extremely heavy door. Indeed, the door is so heavy that small children and older people have difficulty opening it. On several

occasions I have had to open it for older people because they have been unable to pull it back.
After getting through the original difficulty presented by the door one reaches a very dark vestibule having a stone floor. During the winter months, and with the winter conditions we have in southern Ontario, a great deal of ice and snow accumulates with the result that the floor becomes slippery. Last winter I believe one lady broke her hip after sliding and falling on that floor. After crossing the vestibule, if one is fortunate enough to do so without accident, he reaches a small step leading to two swinging doors, only one of which opens inward. I believe both open out. This irregularity is the cause of many bumped noses. To get out one must pass back through either of these two swinging doors and down a step. From the stone step one reaches the vestibule which, as I have said, in winter time is covered with ice and snow and is often slippery. It was at this point that the accident occurred. From the vestibule one passes to the outside.
I would also refer to the mail box placed outside for the posting of letters. Naturally one would expect that a mail box outside a post office, to receive letters and parcels after mailing hours, would be at street level. But we find nothing of the kind in this instance. In this particular post office the box is about floor level above the street. A set of steps has been erected outside the post office so people may reach this slot on the side of the building. These steps were built a few years ago, and have crumbled away to a great extent. They are so narrow, particularly when they are covered with ice and snow in the winter months, that they would accommodate only the feet of a small child. They are exceedingly dangerous; so much so that numerous complaints have been made and people have stated they refuse to go up the steps. The result is that an old fashioned red box has been placed outside to facilitate people wishing to post letters and parcels after hours. However this box is around at the side of the building, and most people do not know it is there.
I bring these matters to the attention of the minister because, while they are small, they are very important to the people who use the post office every day. And, in addition, during the winter months the condition found there could become exceedingly dangerous and hazardous, and already has occasioned one accident. I would recommend that the situation be corrected, and I bring it to the minister's attention.
Thank you.
This would appear to be a sort of safety valve for the department. As the minister has said it is a reserve. I notice the amount is $1,200,000, the same as last year.
That is correct.

However, as indicated at page 448 of the estimates book, the estimated expenditures for 1953-54 are set at $900,000, and the actual expenditures in 1952-53 were $936,015. With a new broom in the Department of Public Works-a nice, new minister and a nice, new deputy-it seems that with all these nice, new heads, and with the promise that we are to have a far more efficient Department of Public Works than we had before, this would have been a good place to begin making a change. If he needed this amount at all, why could he not cut the figure to $1 million. That would have been a saving of at least $200,000, and every $200,000 helps.
The hon. member is not aware of how many items were cut out of the estimates.

That may be so; but here is another that could have been cut-and I hope it will be cut next year. Would the minister explain why this item is necessary at this time, when we have new and efficient management in the department?
Thank you.

Why is it necessary to have this big reserve? I can understand it might have been necessary in the old days when the Department of Public Works was run as a patronage department; but why should these reserves be necessary now? What I say applies not only to item 376 which covers unforeseen improvements but also to item 402, which sets aside another $400,000 for this purpose:
To supplement, on approval of treasury board except where less than $1,000 is required, any of the appropriations of the Department of Public Works.
Obviously that is just another amount held in reserve. And, then, item 403-
That is under the engineering branch.

Item 403 is as follows:
To provide for balances required to complete any projects undertaken in previous fiscal years and for which no specific provision is made in the fiscal year 1954-55, $400,000.
It seems to me that an efficient department could plan with sufficient care that it would not be necessary to have large reserves of this kind set aside every year in the estimates. I would ask the minister to comment on this situation.
Supply-Public Works
Then I would ask the minister to explain to the committee the responsibility of his department with regard to buildings beyond Canada. When the estimates were first under consideration we raised the argument that, as its name implies, the Department of Public Works should be the department of government responsible for public works in Canada. In recent years this country has been spending more and more money on buildings abroad. For example, we have-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must draw to the hon. member's attention the fact that we are discussing item 376, and I am afraid a discussion of public buildings outside Canada does not come within it.
This item is a building item for unforeseen improvements.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
If I may finish-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. May I point out to the hon. member the terms of the resolution? The resolution reads:
Construction, acquisition, major repairs and improvements of, and plans and sites for, public buildings listed in the details of the estimates.
In other words, the discussion under this item is limited to projects which are listed in the details.

My understanding of this vote of $1,200,000 is that it is not restricted to the buildings that are outlined in the details, but it is a reserve to cover any other buildings that may be necessary. The minister can correct me if I am wrong.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not the way in which the resolution reads, but perhaps the minister can help us on that point.

In fact, the minister has already said that such is the case; that this is a reserve of money that may be required to be expended on any buildings. Obviously there would be no point in confining it to the buildings that are actually mentioned because amounts are set out for these particular buildings.
In Canada?
No, buildings anywhere; if it happens to be a building outside Canada then it would come under that vote, Mr. Chairman.

Yes, I should be glad to comment on that, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member's observation was a perfectly valid one. I stated in the house and elsewhere that it is not our intention to put in the estimates amounts of money that we are not likely to

Supply-Public Works spend during the year in question. It is true that last year we did not spend $1,200,000, although that amount was voted.
You did not spend that.

No, I said we did not spend it. This year the officials were able to convince me that we are likely to require $1,200,000. I can assure my hon. friend that if I find we are not spending all of this vote, it will be cut down next year. It is not our intention to ask for votes that we will not be able to spend.
As to the responsibility of the Department of Public Works for buildings abroad, so far the department has had no responsibility for those buildings. At the present time we are engaged in discussions with the Department of External Affairs and it may be that we shall assume some responsibility.
I think that point is of great importance, Mr. Chairman, because as I said earlier more and more money is being spent on buildings abroad.
That is correct.

There is to be a new building at The Hague, a new building in Rome and either a new building or an expansion of a building in Paris. A building is being completed in Washington which last year was supposed, to cost $1 million, and we are now told it is going to cost $2 million. I hold in my hand a dispatch of April 26 of this year headed: "Costly Canadian military headquarters biggest foreign army job in Washington." A swank building is being erected by the Canadian government at a cost of $2 million. The article says:
It is a $2 million stone and steel structure complete with bronze door automatic elevators and a big bomb shelter.
Resting on 900 concrete pegs, each driven 40 feet deep into the soft ground of stately tree-lined Massachusetts avenue, the massive structure was started last fall. It is about one-third completed.
The dispatch goes on to say:
The building will be the largest in Washington designed by a foreign embassy purely for its military components.
Then last October we had the Canadian consul general in New York, Mr. Ray Lawson, getting big ideas about a building for Canada in New York. I am quoting from a dispatch of October 31, 1953:
Canada House in United States to cost $5 million
A $5 million Canada House which would serve as New York headquarters for all major Canadian enterprises-business and governmental-is proposed by Ray Lawson, Canadian consul general here.
It is about time that the Department of Public Works stepped into this picture. They are, or should be, the best qualified to decide


on the kinds of buildings that are going to be erected all over the world by Canada. I suspect quite a few million dollars could be saved for the taxpayers of this country if the Department of Public Works handled all these buildings rather than let the Department of External Affairs put up these swell buildings for their embassies.
Has government policy been changed at all? Has the Department of Public Works been put in charge of the construction of these buildings? I notice from the annual report of the department for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1953, which we now have, and therefore, can no longer complain about not getting the report, that at page 107 the Department of Public Works gets into the picture of those public buildings beyond Canada only for buying the floor wax and things like that. We have here nothing for buildings beyond Canada for construction, but for repairs and maintenance there is $14,000 odd; rent, $72,000. Apparently the Department of External Affairs lets the Department of Public Works pay rents on the buildings that are rented, but does not let it have anything to do with construction. For salaries and wages the amount is about $500; furniture and fittings, $5,200; fuel, about $1,500; light and power, $6,800; water, $2,000; caretakers' supplies and sundries-this is where the floor wax comes in, I suppose-$12,200; total, $115,400 odd. That is the sum and substance of the contribution of the Department of Public Works to Canadian buildings abroad.
Can the minister assure us that his department is to be given a place in this picture and that it will become the authority which constructs the buildings for Canada abroad?

I think I outlined before when the estimates of the department were up earlier in April the general policy regarding the role of the Department of Public Works. I said just a moment ago that we are now engaged in conversations with the Department of External Affairs as to public works' participation in their building programs. What we in the Department of Public Works would like to do is to have the department in that degree of good shape that would make other departments feel we can carry out their construction work to better advantage for them than they can themselves. I would personally hope that would be the case, and it is the goal toward which we are working.
Item agreed to.
May I be permitted to ask a question on item 368 which was passed a few weeks ago?
I do not mind, if there is unanimous consent, so long as it is not a discussion. If it is a question, I do not mind.
This question has to do with construction of a public building in Chicoutimi?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Has the hon. member
unanimous consent to revert to item 368?
Agreed.
An item of $250,000 was approved by parliament last year for that project but nothing has been done up till now. Would the minister care to comment on the project?

The situation there, Mr. Chairman, as I recall it, is that although there was that amount in the estimates last year we found this year when compiling the estimates that we were not ready to go ahead with the building. The plans had not been prepared. At the same time the Postmaster General indicated to me that he would like to study the whole matter of postal services in the area, and until such time as that is done we shall not be able to proceed with the building.
Engineering branch-
377.	Branch administration, $633,824.

I am not quite sure whether I should bring up here what I want to deal with or under item 395. Perhaps the minister can help me. I want to deal with the item that was in last year's estimates for the Vesuvius bay and Crofton ferry and which is out this year. I do not know whether I should discuss it here or whether I should wait until we come to item 395. If the minister does not object to my dealing with it under this item, I will do so now.
I should be glad to have it dealt with under this item. If my hon. friend would like me to do so, I can tell him quickly what the situation is.
Yes; if the minister will.

Last year in the estimates- I think it was in the supplementary estimates -there was an amount to cover ferry landings at both Crofton and Vesuvius bay to accommodate a ferry which was to be purchased privately, I believe, and operated under a subsidy provided by the provincial government. When I considered these estimates it seemed to me that that was appropriately a matter for the provincial government because the ferry service is really
Supply-Public Works
an extension of the highway service of the provincial government. We therefore dropped the item pending further consideration. I have now had an opportunity of considering the projects in detail and also of discussing them with the minister of public works of British Columbia. I believe there are grounds now for considering them as joint projects. I believe the ferry landings can be regarded in the nature of public wharfs with structures built to them to accommodate a ferry. I told the minister of public works of British Columbia that I thought it was a matter with regard to which we could appropriately co-operate to the advantage of the citizens who wished to use the service. With that in mind, I propose to ask treasury board to include in the supplementary estimates amounts for ferry landings both at Crofton and at Vesuvius bay.
Thank you.

As this is the first item under the engineering branch, can the minister tell us the present position with regard to work on Ripple rock? Some weeks ago we had a report that there had been a core taken of the rock underneath the narrows and up under Ripple rock to see whether or not the water would break into a tunnel if one were constructed. Can the minister tell us whether a report has yet been received on the results?

I am sorry that I am not in
a position to do so. My hon. friend will recall that when this recent approach to the removal of Ripple rock was brought forward the responsibility was transferred from the Minister of Public Works to the national research council which is under the jurisdiction of my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I am aware in a general way of the work that has been done but I assume that my friend will wish to get the details from my colleague. I have not them in my possession.
If it is decided to bore the tunnel out under the narrows and up so that the rock can be blown up, will that work be done by the research council or by the Department of Public Works?
I would think it would be done by the Department of Public Works but as yet there has been no determination of that matter.

Item agreed to.
Dredging-
380. Maintenance and operation of plant and contract and day labour works, $3,674,565.

Under this item I notice an appropriation or estimate of $3,674,565
4242	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works
tor maintenance and operation of plant and contract and day labour works for dredging. Out of this total I am pleased to note that a sum of $1,291,552 will be spent for dredging in the maritime provinces.
May I be permitted to describe briefly the situation which exists in my county where the fishing industry is of major importance. The one thousand or more fishermen of Gloucester county land commercially twenty-four different varieties of fish and shellfish. Unfortunately ice conditions from December to May prevent fishing operations during these months, with the exception of smelt fishing which is carried on through the ice. It is therefore most important that these hard-working fishermen be provided with facilities allowing them to take full advantage of the short period of six months where they have to earn a full year's living for themselves and their large families.
Harbours and channels with sufficient depth of water are required to permit those deep-sea fishermen, equipped with modern craft, to reach the fishing grounds and to return to port with their catches. If the fishing industry is to survive it is essential that these fishermen be provided with facilities to navigate freely at all tides, under all kinds of weather conditions at least during the summer months.
The entire Gloucester county deep-sea fishing fleet, including over 50 modern draggers, valued at over $lf million, uses the entrance of Shippigan gully between the mainland and Shippigan island, on their way to and returning from the fishing grounds. Day in and day out, at all hours of the day or night, under most favourable weather conditions as well as during heavy gales, storms or fog, these sturdy fishermen have to feel their way through a winding and twisting channel to reach their ultimate destination.
I want to take advantage of this opportunity to impress upon the Minister of Public Works the urgent need for immediate action on this particular project. Unless the dredging of the main channel at the entrance of Shippigan harbour is proceeded with without delay, a proportion of the fishing fleet will be most seriously handicapped during the coming fishing season. A total catch involving approximately 40 million pounds of fish deserves the utmost attention of the department.
This request, Mr. Chairman, also applies to a number of harbours along the Gloucester county coast line. How can we expect those brave fishermen to exploit to the best of their ability the rich resources of the sea if they have to wait for long hours, and sometimes for days, for the tide to rise so as to enable them to refloat their grounded fishing vessels? I would appreciate it, as would
[Mr. Robichaud.1

my friends the fishermen, if the minister could assure the committee that he will give this request the attention it deserves and would ask his department to recognize its urgency.
I shall certainly be glad to give to that request the attention that I am glad to give to all hon. members' requests.

At page 453 we find the details of this vote. There is an increase in redredging by contract or day labour of $100,000 and there is an increase in repairs and upkeep of equipment of approximately $130,000. Why is it necessary to have these big increases in these items?

Redredging by contract or day labour amounting to $675,000 provides for maintenance dredging by companies when the work cannot be carried out by departmental plant due to the fact that departmental dredges are unable to perform all of the dredging operations; in other cases, when redredging is needed in areas some distance from the department's dredging fleet and includes particular cases where annual redredging is required. It also covers small day labour redredging jobs by scraper, bulldozer, drag lines, hand dredging and so on. The reason for the increase here is that the amount voted last year was not enough to cover the work we were required to do. We ran short of funds. This year we want to make sure we have enough.
How much was spent last year?
I have not that figure before me. I am told the amount was fully encumbered but we have not been able to spend the amount of money we expected would be required to be spent during the year.
Why is it going to cost $120,000 more to repair equipment this year than it did last year?
These are increases for the maintenance of new plants to be put into operation in 1954-55, $33,000.
But that is capital expenditure and surely would not come under the heading of repair?

It is for the maintenance of new plants being put into operation. The second item deals with the replacement of boilers for dredge No. 9 and tug Fredericton, $60,000; replacement of five pontoons for dredge No. 21, $38,600; replacement of pontoons for dredge No. 305, $20,000, which makes a total of $151,600 less decreases in other plants which amount to $19,757 leaving a net increase of $131,843.

Can the minister explain which department does this dredging? I believe this is another case where work has been taken away from the Department of Public Works and is being done by other departments. For example, a great deal of dredging is being done by the Department of Transport. Can the minister explain why it is necessary to have any department, other than his own department, do dredging work in Canada, and to what extent other departments are doing dredging work, and what the basis is for this division? It does seem to me it would be more efficient if the Department of Public Works could handle this type of work.

I might say at the outset that the work is all done by the Department of Public Works with the exception of the St. Lawrence ship channel and the canals such as the Rideau canal, the Lachine canal and others which are under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport.
But why cannot your department dredge the Rideau canal?
There is no reason why we cannot do this. It is just a division of responsibility and I would not care to comment on whether it is more efficient.
Is there any real reason why this dredging cannot be done by the Department of Public Works?
It is simply that the ship channels and canals come under their jurisdiction and I suppose it has been a matter of practice for them to carry out the work.

But the Fraser river carries a great deal of shipping.
Mr. 'Winters: I know.
And the dredging there is done by the Department of Public Works.
I would not wish to argue the merits of this with my hon. friend. It is a matter of practice.
Does the minister really feel that this dredging should be done by his own department?
I would not wish to comment on that.

Item agreed to.
Roads and bridges-
384.	Maintenance and operation, $423,449.

Mr. Chairman, this item concerns the Burlington channel bridge and there is an item in the details concerning that bridge amounting to $85,920 concerning maintenance and operation. Which bridge does that cover?
Supply-Public Works
That is the highway bascule bridge.
Has there been any progress made in connection with the proposed new bridge over the last few weeks?

Perhaps I can best answer that by reading a letter which I dispatched to the minister of highways for the province of Ontario on April 5, 1954. That is the last communication I have on the matter. I had a brief discussion with the minister of highways, Mr. Doucett, one day last week though it added nothing to the matter and was merely a passing conversation. This is the letter:
Dear Mr. Doucett:
This is with reference to your letter dated February 15, 1954, in which you requested federal financial participation in the building of a high level four-lane vehicular bridge over the Burlington canal.
Although engineering plans have not yet been submitted to us, and, as a result, there is no detailed estimate of costs, we understand that your preliminary estimate of that part of the bridge toward which you feel the federal government might participate is $13,300,000. This, of course, is subject to change when the detailed plans are available, but I understand you feel it may nevertheless be regarded as a good preliminary estimate.
This whole matter has received careful consideration by this department and by the government. I believe it is generally recognized that the problem is primarily one of facilitating the flow of highway traffic which has increased substantially in the past few years and which is likely to grow further in the future. If we were mutually concerned only with local vehicular traffic, then a much less expensive bridge than the one you are now contemplating would be satisfactory. In fact, the double bascule bridge built and operated by the federal government would serve the purpose.
However, the federal government is appreciative of your desire to provide facilities for an increased flow of vehicular traffic, and since part of the cost at any rate is due to the requirements of navigation which make a high level bridge necessary, the federal government feels there is some justification for its financial participation.
Having regard to the fact that this problem is primarily one of handling highway traffic within the province, it follows that it falls within the scope of provincial jurisdiction. However, because of the factors mentioned above, the federal government has authorized me to inform you that it is prepared to contribute up to one-third of the cost of a high level bridge.
I understand from our previous conversation that your government will assume full responsibility for highway traffic over the canal and that once the high level bridge is completed it will no longer be necessary for the federal government to maintain and operate the bascule bridge which we would then remove. At the same time, as a matter of convenience to pedestrian traffic, we propose to add to the present railway bridge a sidewalk or sidewalks to enable pedestrians to pass from one side of the canal to the other.
You may wish to inform me if the foregoing terms on which the federal government is prepared to participate are satisfactory to you.
(Signed) Robert H. Winters

Supply-Public Works
You have not received anything from the provincial government since?
No.

Well, I think it is about time you did because, as the hon. member for Niagara Falls pointed out a few days ago, this is the biggest bottleneck in Canada and possibly the biggest on the North American continent. I do not believe there should be any great delay in starting this bridge because at the present time there is considerable delay every time a pleasure cruiser wishes to go from the lake to Hamilton harbour. Traffic is held up and it is a very great nuisance. If the provincial government is at fault then I think it is about time they started doing something about this situation.

Mr. Chairman, this item mentions the Burlington channel bridge, the Kingston, LaSalle causeway and the New Westminster bridge. Can the minister tell us the basis on which the dominion accepts responsibility for the Kingston, LaSalle causeway and the New Westminster bridge?

Mr. Chairman, I am not aware of that. This matter has not risen before and I have not had an opportunity of looking into the background or the basis on which we are participants. I am therefore not in a position to say. However, if my hon. friend would like me to look into the matter and discuss it with him I would be glad to do so.

I shall be grateful if the minister will do that.
Item carried.
Roads and bridges-
385.	Towards international bridge over the St. Croix river between St. Stephen, New Brunswick, and Calais, Maine, the state of Maine to pay a like amount, $125,000.
Can the minister tell us when he expects this work on the international bridge to be completed?

That is thinking in the future. We have not even arrived at a final decision with the state of Maine as to its start, let alone its completion. But we are making progress. We have seen preliminary designs of the bridge. We have agreed now that it should be a two-lane bridge. There was quite a responsible body of opinion locally which felt it should be a four-lane bridge. We explored the matter with the United States authorities to find out whether or not they were interested in a four-lane bridge and would participate in the cost of it, but we concluded that faster action would result if we stuck to a two-lane bridge. Plans are now in the process of being prepared. I hope they will be ready before too long.
I think the minister should press for a four-lane bridge and not give up too easily.
We were quite prepared to press. As a matter of fact, we did press, but when there is a partnership it takes more than the pressure of one partner to bring about a satisfactory conclusion.
That is true in more cases than bridges.

Item agreed to.
Roads and bridges-
386.	Towards construction of spans of bridge over the interprovincial channel of the Ottawa river between Pembroke, Ontario, and Allumette island, Quebec, $200,000.
This is a contribution towards a bridge to be built across the Ottawa river?
That is right.
Will the minister explain the basis on which the dominion accepts responsibility for helping to build that bridge, and also the division of cost?

Yes, I would be very glad to do that. The basis on which we accept some responsibility is that it is an interprovincial river. It is the Ottawa river and any bridge crossing it would reach from the province of Ontario to the province of Quebec. Under the British North America Act the federal government has some responsibility for interprovincial bridges where such bridges are required to be built. As to the sharing of the cost, that is still a matter for decision. We have had discussions with the appropriate officials of Ontario and Quebec. We are prepared to be quite flexible and have already said that we would participate on two bases of costs which were submitted by the other partners.
One of them was that there should be a straight split of one-third. We said we would agree to that. One of the other partners suggested that Quebec do a portion of the work, Ontario do a portion of the work and we do the balance of the work, roughly the centre section. We said we were prepared to agree if that was the basis on which it was finally to be worked out. The three partners have not yet come to a final decision whether the bridge should be built or on what basis the costs of the structure should be shared. I am hopeful that we will reach agreement. I feel that the other two partners are interested in getting on with the job. It was only this week that I exchanged letters with the premier of Quebec on this important matter in the hope that we can come to some early decision.
What is the estimated cost of the bridge?
I think it is of the order of $1,200,000 or $1,300,000.
Is it a high level bridge?
No, it is not a high level bridge.

The minister stated that the responsibility of the federal government was defined under the British North America Act. My understanding, for which my authority is the former premier of New Brunswick, Mr. McNair, is that the federal government is responsible for the whole cost of building interprovincial bridges. I brought the matter up here a few years ago. I asked for an opinion from the Department of Justice but I never received one. It was in connection with the Campbellton-Cross Point bridge between New Brunswick and Quebec. I also understand that the provincial governments of New Brunswick and Quebec still feel that the responsibility is that of the federal government and that it is set out in the British North America Act along those lines. I wonder whether the minister has any comments to make on that or whether he is definitely of the opinion that the responsibility of each government is limited to one-third?

No, I have no strong views on the subject. I think these are matters which require negotiation. It is all right to say that a certain bridge should be a federal responsibility but if that does not produce a bridge it does not do anybody any good.
Is the matter clearly defined in the British North America Act?

I am no expert on the British North America Act. I understand there is some federal responsibility where a bridge is international or interprovincial. I understand too that there is also the question of how much of an interprovincial bridge is actually interprovincial because up to the boundary it is within one province and on the other side of the boundary it is within the other province. It is a very difficult problem and I do not profess to be able to offer a solution to it.
Just another argument for a federal-provincial conference.
An argument for federal-provincial co-operation.

Item agreed to.
Acquisition, construction and improvements of
harbour and river works-
388.	Nova Scotia, $4,923,000.

There is a question I want to ask the minister. The details of this item are on page 460 and there is an amount for
Supply-Public Works
dredging for Sydney, Nova Scotia. I am wondering whether that is dredging of the harbour or a sandbar outside the harbour. The amount that the federal government is spending is $37,000 and I am wondering who is paying the rest and just what kind of dredging project it is.

This $37,000 is 50 per cent of the estimated cost of the dredging. The Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation will pay the other 50 per cent of the cost. The dredging of berthing areas is necessary to provide sufficient depth for large ocean-going cargo boats chartered by the Dominion Iron and Steel corporation and the Dominion Coal Company for import and export shipments of steel, coal and iron ore. The proposed work is:	(a) dredging berth west side of coal
loading pier No. 2; (b) dredging berths east and west side coal loading pier No. 3; (c) dredging berths east and west side steel loading pier No. 1; and (d) dredging berths east and west side ore loading pier No. 2. The above dredging involves the removal of 48,000 cubic yards, scow measurement, of sand, silt, clay and gravel.
Is the work to be done by the department's dredging apparatus or by a private firm?
The work is to be done by contract.
By your own dredges?
No, we will invite tenders and let a contract. That is the intention.

I should like to make a general comment on these items. Looking at the general items for the engineering branch, it is obvious that there is a great saving in this particular work. In 1953-54 $34,612,500 was spent, and the amount for 1954-55 is $25,820,600, a saving of $8,791,900. We are always very pleased indeed to note savings of this kind, but it does seem rather peculiar that last year there was an expenditure of over $8 million more than it is intended to spend this year. I mention this because, speaking particularly of my own province- and I know that the same conditions prevail in other provinces-we are in a recession. The provincial government of New Brunswick is endeavouring to find provincial works in order to relieve the unemployment situation there. When I was home at Easter I met people practically at every turn wanting to know what the provincial government was going to do on this road, that road and the other road in order to give employment to the people.
Now, as I said a moment ago, it is an anomalous situation that the federal government, when there is a recession in this
4246	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works
country and when there are over half a million people unemployed, should reduce the amount of the expenditure for public works of this kind in which employment could be given. I am going to be blunt about it. In the election year there was some $34 million expended when the employment situation was not nearly as bad as it is today, when there is a decrease of over $9 million.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, this is something that requires some explanation from the government. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Gloucester mention his constituency a few minutes ago. We know what the situation has been in Gloucester county because the former member for Gloucester was a strong advocate of public works in his constituency.
He was not better than this one.
I am not making any invidious comparison, I am only stating the facts.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I am afraid the time has come when I must interrupt the hon. member on the ground that a discussion as to whether or not the policies of the Department of Public Works should be directed towards relieving unemployment was, I think, properly held under the general administration item. We are now dealing with specific items which deal with specific dredging in various places. I am not trying to curtail discussion any more than is absolutely necessary for the efficient carrying out of the business of the committee.
I am going to ask hon. members now that we have passed the general item to try to confine their discussions to the items that we have before us. I know that the initial items on this dredging were called rather quickly and perhaps the hon. member who now has the floor did not have an opportunity to get up on the original dredging item. I am going to say at this stage that it is my opinion that a general debate on the question of whether or not public works should be used as a means of relieving unemployment is not in order on the item now before us.

I have to bow, of course, to your ruling. I still cannot help noticing the great difference there is in the amount voted in this item this year as compared to last year. I do not believe it is out of place to comment on the necessity for this work this year as compared with last year. Take my own province, for instance, and we find that in 1953-54 under item 390 there was $2,880,000 voted for work that year, whereas this year the amount is $1,334,500, a difference of $1,545,000.


While I am not going to discuss the matter any farther, I am sure it is obvious to every member in this house, and it is certainly obvious to the people concerned, that there is an anomalous situation. Take Prince Edward Island, for instance. We find under item 389 the vote this year is $847,800, whereas last year it was $1,930,000, a difference of $1,082,200 for that small province. I do feel that the house and the country are entitled to some explanation as to why there is such a large difference in the vote this year as compared with last year.
I should be very glad to say a few words. I am always interested in the way my hon. friend sees political significance in everything we do.
It is so obvious.

He looks for a political reason behind every bush. I often have to disappoint him. This is not the first time I have had to disappoint him this year by asserting that there is no political significance in the point he has raised. I hate to have to do it again, but that is the fact. I must say that my friend is one of those who, in an election campaign, speak most vigorously about the high level of government spending, but the moment it drops he says, "Let it drop somewhere else, but not here."
You have never heard me say that.

I read some of your reported speeches last year. Of the total amount voted, which my hon. friend says correctly was $34,612,500, the total amount spent was about $21-5 million. Now, as I told my hon. friend before, it is our policy to try to include in the estimates only the amounts we expect to be able to spend. If we can spend this $25,820,000 it will actually represent an increase rather than a decrease. I hope that will help to allay the haunting fears of my good friend.
I hope it will give some employment.

Item agreed to.
Acquisition, construction and improvements of harbour and river works-
389.	Prince Edward Island, $847,800.

I have a question or two to ask on this item. I notice in connection with the vote for harbour investigation and development at Rustico, last year the amount was $100,000 and there is an indication in the note that of the $150,000 in the estimates this year $90,000 is a revote. I take it that only $10,000 was actually spent out of the $100,000 voted last year?
That is correct, Mr. Chairman.

I trust the minister will be able to assure us that this year the course of events will be different and a real attempt will be made to carry on this project so that the $150,000 will be spent for improvements.
That is our aim, Mr. Chairman.

I have one other question. Can the minister indicate whether any request has reached him with regard to a wharf at Point Prim for use of the rather large number of fishermen who fish from that point? I did not see any item in the estimates, and I was wondering if it might be covered in the supplementaries?

The item was requested, and I know it has been requested several times by the junior member for Queens, but we were not in a position to go forward with it because we had not completed our investigations and have not been able to do any planning.

I wonder whether the
minister could give the details of that $150,000 expenditure at Rustico?

This amount of $150,000
includes a $90,000 revote, and is required to continue the investigation for the development of the harbour and to provide funds for actual construction as indicated by the investigation to be necessary. An amount of $36,000 is included in this item for the construction of a boat shelter now under contract with Messrs. Noye, Raynor and Noye. Improvement and development of Rustico harbour in the interests of the fishing industry is an immediate necessity.
A survey of the tides, currents and sea bed movements in the area was carried out in 1953 by the Nova Scotia technical science service under the direction of Dr. S. J. Mazur at a cost of about $20,000. Rustico harbour is one of the most important fishing stations in the province, activity being carried on continuously from the opening of the lobster season, May 1, up to the close of cod and mackerel season in the late fall. The proposed work, as I indicated, is for a boat shelter, now under contract, and the building of a dam to shut off Little harbour at the east end of Robinson's island; and possible further surveys, as well as to carry out any other recommended improvements based on the findings of the investigations carried out in the past two years.

I see an item of $17,500 for a wharf at Little Pokemouche gully. Can the minister tell us when the department intends to call tenders for this project?
We are still awaiting the results of borings for that project.

I have a few questions to ask about breakwaters in the bay of Fundy, Saint John county. I believe I have already indicated to the minister the concern of the people of Lorneville about their breakwater. It is spring in that area now, and work has not yet begun. They are wondering what the plans are for the breakwater at Lorneville.

I have asked the department to engage the services of a consulting engineer to carry out an inspection and make a report. For this purpose we have retained Mr. O. J. McCulloch, who is a consultant in the marine field. I understand he has visited the breakwater but I have not yet received his report.

I would remind the minister that the breakwater in its present condition is of no use to the fishermen down there. They have been very patient about the matter and would like to see some action taken this spring.
That is why I thought I should get a report on it.

I would also inquire about the situation at Dipper Harbour. I am given to understand-and I have seen for myself-that the old retaining wall, which has been used partly as a breakwater, is now giving way. The residents indicate that a few dollars spent now would serve the purpose, but that if it is left until a later time it would require the expenditure of a large amount of money. Is there any report on this breakwater?
I have no report before me, but I shall consider my hon. friend's comments.

I wish the minister would do so, because promises were made two or three years ago that something would be done, and a small expenditure now would probably save considerable expense in the future.
Then, what is the plan for Maces Bay, for which there is an amount this year?
We expect to have the plans ready for the breakwater extension at Maces Bay within the next few days.

Then, I would ask about dredging at Courtenay bay in Saint John harbour. I am bringing the matter up at this time,

Supply-Public Works
because amounts have been spent for this purpose in other years. There is a story around Saint John that the new oil tankers cannot enter Courtenay bay because dredging has been slowed up. What are the intentions for the future at that point?

At the request of the Irving Oil Company, and certain other citizens in Saint John, including my hon. friend's predecessor in the house, we have been studying the situation. We have not yet made any final decision, and we have no funds in the estimates for work at Courtenay bay.

I would ask the minister to keep in mind the fact that we have always had these oil companies located at Saint John, but that recently moves have been made to Halifax to accommodate part of their facility. We do not know for sure if it is the policy of the companies or merely because the facilities at Saint John are not extensive enough to provide proper docking and harbour facilities to service a modern tanker fleet. I hope we will not lose out in this connection merely because of a few dollars in the estimates.

Item agreed to.
