This item refers to the work of the engineering branch in Ontario. I would ask the minister whether his department has any administrative control over or any interest in the water level of lake Nipissing. I have before me correspondence from individuals and recommendations from chambers of commerce and city councils regarding the low level of water in that lake. Has this matter been discussed, and what can be done?

There is a control dam at the outlet of the French river into lake Nipissing, which is owned by the Department of Public Works; and we exercise control over the level of water. A deputation was received recently from North Bay in connection with this problem and we are keeping active supervision of control measures. We receive water levels reports twice daily, and are endeavouring to see that the situation is controlled to the best advantage.

Mr. Chairman, in the riding of Bruce there is a shore line of about 150 miles. There can be no doubt that on many occasions the requirements along the shore line could become a headache for the Department of Public Works. However, I would ask the minister for some

information concerning the proposed construction of a dock at Tobermory. I understand that in years gone by there was an estimate for part of this work. This year it is dropped completely. I would point out that there are many people in that locality who depend on fishing for a livelihood. Then, I am sure the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is familiar with the area, and will know about the beautiful scenery in that part of Ontario.
To complete the work some 900 feet would have to be constructed. My suggestion is that, when the minister's department reaches the point of building the dock, it should not be done piecemeal. I ask the minister not to do it piecemeal. When you take into consideration the amount of money that will be spent, it will be more economical to do it all at once. Eleven fishing boats worked out of the harbour of Tobermory and last year they sold $212,448 worth of fish. I am sure the minister is familiar with marine slips, and if he will visit that area he will agree with what I am saying. Can the minister tell us whether at the present time they have plans in view for future construction?

I understand my hon. friend is talking about the proposed dock at Tobermory. There was an item of $50,000 in the estimates last year. We have not been able to decide upon a proper site because of differences of opinion locally, nor have we obtained the water lot, but we do hope to be able to proceed with the project there. It is still in the planning stage, and that is all I can tell my hon. friend at this time.

Once more I would ask the minister not to consider doing it piecemeal, but all at once. Is the department contemplating doing any permanent work at Southampton in connection with the river mouth? It is a bone of contention every year, and it costs a lot of money for dredging.
In the details of the estimates there is an item on page 466 which reads: "Saugeen river (Southampton)-reconstruction of pier." The amount is $110,000.

In connection with that, I understand a deputation will be coming down to have an interview with the minister which I am sure they will obtain. Their suggestions will be worth taking into consideration in regard to permanently improving the river mouth. It may entail some cooperation between the municipality and the province, I do not know; but I would suggest that it be looked into from that view to make something permanent.

Since my riding of Danforth is adjacent to York-Scarborough, similar conditions exist on its shore line. Erosion is taking place from the currents of water going both east and west under certain adverse weather conditions. May we have the details of how the money is to be allotted?

As to Scarborough bluffs, except for what the hon. member has told me, we have had no deputations or any requests for any action there. I understand it is the general problem of erosion in areas of the great lakes.

Erosion is caused by the current, as pointed out by the hon. member for York-Scarborough, and it has been taking place for a good number of years. About twenty years ago they did take care of the south end of the riding toward the westerly part. It was suffering from the same kind of erosion at that time, and they did a fairly good job. But at the east end of the riding and also in York-Scarborough, which includes the Scarborough bluffs, there is a serious problem that will have to be attended to. Only a limited amount of money will be available. The money that the minister has reference to goes to harbour improvements within the Toronto bay proper. It has to do with channels leading to the bay and so forth. This condition is outside of the bay altogether. No provision has been made this year for taking care of the erosion on lake Ontario. Is it possible to get an appropriation for that?

This problem of erosion comes up every year, and every year the government states its position. The general policy is that unless the erosion is attributable to navigation, or is likely to endanger navigation, or is caused by some federal government structure, then it is not a federal government responsibility.

I realize that. The last time assistance was given, I believe, on a joint proposition between the province, the municipality and the federal authorities, and it was done through the hon. member for Danforth at that time. Probably the same arrangement could be made at this time.
I presume that was one of those unemployment relief measures in the early 1930's.
If we have the same condition now it would apply again.
The erosion or the unemployment relief measure?

What I am anxious about is something to take care of the erosion condition that exists, and if it cannot be done this year I should like to have something earmarked for this problem next year.

Mr. Pallet!: Can the minister tell me what work he expects to have completed on the Port Credit harbour this year? In the estimates $400,000 is earmarked for that work. I wonder just what it entails.
I have read some of my hon. friend's advertisements in his election campaign. I presume it is related to them. It is a revote.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister sees politics behind every bush.

I did not see it first. It is a revote of $400,000 to provide towards harbour improvements to give deep-water facilities to serve the growing industrial area between Toronto and Hamilton. This is a breakdown of it. The entire proposal includes the construction of a breakwater, several wharves, a slip and approach, and dredging to give deep draught harbourage.

In the details there is a revote of $20,000 for Blockhouse island at Brock-ville. Can the minister give me information as to what the department has in mind with regard to the work at Blockhouse island?

The proposed work is demolition of the existing cribwork structure down to low-water level; the building up of the east bank of the island with stone fill; the laying of an 18-inch concrete mat over this fill; the construction of a masonry wall with a one to one slope up to elevation 248-3; the laying of a 10-inch pavement slab.
Mr. Pallet!: The original question I asked the minister was as to the work which it was expected would be completed this year. I may have misunderstood the minister but I do not quite feel the answer was given to that question. I refer to Port Credit harbour.
We expect to start with one wharf this year.

(Mr. Small.!

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I have one other question under the general heading of work in the province of Manitoba. I ask this question because of the discussion a moment ago in which the two members from the Toronto area took part. I refer to the discussion as to federal responsibility or denial of responsibility where there is erosion.
As the minister probably knows, a few years ago when his predecessor was minister of public works, some work was finally done at the town of Gimli on the west shore of lake Manitoba. Erosion was taking place there to a considerable extent and it was having an extremely serious effect on the town of Gimli. It was finally admitted by the government that navigation had something to do with it and some valuable work was done. A substantial wall has been built from the centre to the south end of the town. I know that the minister feels that, when something has been done, we in the opposition always say that the government should have done a little bit more. I hope the fact that I seem to be speaking in this vein will not be held against the validity of the claim of the people in that area.
The fact is that the people who have property just south of where that wall was built feel that the further erosion that is taking place with respect to their property is in part due to the currents that are set up by that wall. I know that the minister might say that if the wall were extended a little bit further, those still further south would have a claim. I know something of the geography of that area. I think it is clear that there is a further point to which that wall could be built beyond which it would not be necessary to go further. I hope that the request these people are making for an extension of that wall will be given favourable consideration.
I shall be glad to look into that matter.

Item agreed to.
Acquisition, construction and improvements of harbour and river works-
395.	British Columbia and Yukon, $4,998,500.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make a few remarks under this item. I do not rise by any means in a complaining spirit. I am going to try to make some constructive suggestions, and comments. I know the department is preparing to undertake a good deal of necessary construction and a number of necessary repairs to wharves and structures of that type in my constituency. I want to say that those communities which

will be affected by those new structures or by those improvements appreciate greatly the works proposed by the department.
Before passing on I should like to bring to the minister's attention the fact-and I think 1 am correct in my statement-that I represent a riding that has the highest per capita wealth production in Canada. I think that statement will be found to be correct, if you take the total production of Kootenay West and relate it to the population. This means an extremely large income tax collection from the area. Hence there is great justification for the investment of government funds in public works and facilities of that sort.
I want to bring to the minister's attention the necessity for the reconstruction of a wharf at Robson. I am not expecting that it will be undertaken this year, but I have been asked by the West Kootenay and central farmers' institute, various fruit growers' organizations and the Castlegar chamber of commerce and local residents to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that the old wharf at East Robson is getting extremely shaky. It has been there for a good many years. In fact, it is so shaky now that when the bus goes down to meet the steamer or when the fruit trucks go down to take fruit away from a barge or boat the drivers are told to proceed only part way down because it is not safe to go down the full length. It is certainly not safe for heavy loads at the present time. It is an important wharf because it is the one at East Robson which is at the south end of the Arrow lakes and there is a great deal of tonnage that goes over that wharf throughout the year. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister and his officials in the hope that consideration will be given to the necessity for the reconstruction of this wharf in the near future. I am of the opinion that when the question of reconstruction comes up it will possibly be to the advantage of the public generally to slightly alter the site and possibly construct a somewhat different type of wharf. That is all I am going to say about that. As a matter of fact, the minister knows I ask for very little. I am one of those who bother him very little indeed.
But I want to mention a very important matter in relation to the Duncan river. For some years the department tried to move a large log jam on the Duncan river, as it flows from Howser lake into the north arm of Kootenay lake, but without much success. This meant it was impossible to float booms of logs down the river and impossible for small craft to proceed up river. But finally the department decided to make a new channel after going over the whole question
Supply-Public Works
very thoroughly with one of the minister's engineers who came from New Westminster to discuss and plan what should be done to remedy the situation and the work was finally got under way. I wish to compliment those men who have undertaken the building of that new channel from Howser lake to north Kootenay lake. I believe the cost has been on the average some $4,000 or $5,000 per year. It has been of great convenience to the lumber companies in that area and for small craft proceeding up the river to Howser lake.
However, I wish to make one suggestion relating to this new channel on the Duncan river. In 1896 there was a race between Jim Hill of the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. in regard to the building of a railway into the Lardeau. The C.P.R. got through first, though the railway has since disappeared. However, Jim Hill's engineers built a trestle across Howser lake towards Howser. The grade was built, trestles erected, but the entire project was abandoned when the C.P.R. won the race. Over the years logs and brush, the stumps of trees and debris have floated down from the north Duncan river into Howser lake. That debris has piled up against the piles driven across the south end of Howser lake and there is now a considerable quantity of sand lying against these piles so that the level of Howser lake is being artificially raised more and more each year. That sand has piled up and is causing inconvenience to lumber operators and the few residents living around the lake. I have looked over the whole jam myself with some of the local residents. The current is strong at this point and I would suggest that half a dozen cases of dynamite could be used to blow a hole in this sandbank created by debris accumulated around the pile that would open up a narrow channel but the natural erosion would clear away the rest. I bring this to the minister's attention because I believe that this work could be done with the expenditure of very little money and be a great improvement.

Mr. Chairman, there is one item in this vote on which I would like to question the minister and that is in relation to the fishing harbour at Vancouver. I notice that in the estimates it is referred to as a "fishing harbour". I know it by the more modest name of a wharf. This project has been under request for some considerable time, but I understand there has been difficulty in obtaining control of the property on which to build a wharf. I would like to know what progress has been made during last year. I understand a site has to be
4252	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works
bought from the Indian reservation. I would like the minister to tell us what progress has been made in getting this wharf or harbour completed.

Mr. Chairman, we have
acquired the property on which to build this wharf but as yet we have reached no agreement with the harbour commission as to its management. When that is completed we will be able to proceed with the work for which this money is voted.

Have the plans for the construction of the wharf been completed, and what will be the total cost? Is the total cost included in this estimate? While the minister is dealing with that point he might give us an estimate of when the work might be finished. There is great demand for this harbour on the part of fishermen and fishing vessel owners who come into Vancouver.

The estimated total cost of the fishing harbour is broken down as follows: purchase of land, $90,000; access road, $10,000; dredging, $355,000; bulkhead, shed, roads, parking area, services, platforms, Wharf, etc., $355,500; floats, mooring piles and gangways, $103,750, or a total cost of $914,250. The plans have been prepared and we will be ready to go ahead as soon as the matter of management can be worked out satisfactorily.
On that point the minister said the total cost would be about $914,000.
The total estimated cost, yes.
I take it that includes the $100,000 vote made last year?
That is right.
And the vote for this year of $365,000?
That is correct.
So it is quite apparent that the wharf will not be completed this year?
That is correct.
When does the minister expect it will be finished?

It is difficult to say. We have not yet got the management agreement worked out but as soon as that is arranged we will be ready to get on with the job. I believe if we get on with it reasonably early this year we can complete it in the next fiscal year.
Then the minister believes it will be completed some time in 1955?
Yes.

I put that question because I have here a publication called "Soundings" which is issued by the fishing vessel owners association of British Columbia. The issue for August, 1953, carries the heading "Complete in '54" and the subheading "Funds Assured for Wharf." The article reads: Vancouver's new fisherman's wharf, to be constructed on the south shore of False creek, will be completed and in operation by the fall of 1954.
This is the post-election assurance given by Fisheries Minister James Sinclair.
He said that the additional $625,000 required to complete the development, definitely will be appropriated at the next session of parliament.
Apparently that statement by the minister is incorrect?

I have not spoken to the minister and I do not know under what condition he made that statement. Of course, that is merely a report of what he said. The circumstances are as I have outlined them here today.
The actual fact is that the wharf cannot be completed until 1955?
Yes, that is correct.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask the minister a question regarding dredging in the Fraser river. Earlier this week in a private discussion with him I drew to his attention the problem now being encountered in the Ladner channel in permitting boats in and out of that particular region. At that time I did not have the facts available to substantiate what I was then telling the minister, but I have now obtained the facts and figures from the board of trade of that town and it appears that something like $735,000 worth of shipping passes through. There are four marine gas stations also located there. It is very difficult for a boat to get in and out of the port in order to load and unload its wares. I wonder whether the minister is prepared at this time to state whether they intend to carry on the dredging operations before the spring shipping pressure hits the port?
I take it my hon. friend is speaking of Ladner. No, I am not prepared to state that. I have not the final report.

I have been watching for a place to make inquiries about a certain matter and it would seem to me that it would come under this particular section. It has to do with rock work on West Nicomen island. I have just received a telegram today and perhaps the best thing I could do would be to read it. It reads as follows:
Letter last year from Minister of Public Works advised that a request for rock work on West Nicomen Island cost to be shared equally by federal and provincial and Nicomen district would be

favourably received. This March request made district agreed to raise one-third of cost and the provincial government also agreed to one-third. No reply has been received from federal public works. Due to urgency and the fact that work must be completed before river rises operations have been started but will have to be shut down if immediate reply not received from dominion public works. Could you contact the minister and impress the Importance of a reply being sent in answer to wire to him from provincial diking commission also from deputy minister of lands?
Would the hon. member say who signed the wire?
J. A. Worth, secretary of the West Nicomen ratepayers association at Deroche.
What is the date of it?
April 29. I was wondering whether this project was included in the estimates or whether any action is being taken on the matter.
It is not included in the estimates. We are still studying it.
In view of the urgency of the matter, will the minister be able to give a reply in the very near future?
We will reply very soon.

There is included in this vote an item of $1,080,000 for dredging the first narrows in Vancouver harbour, and that includes a revote of $750,000 which was the total amount of the vote for the preceding fiscal year. I know that considerable work has been done there during the last fiscal year. How was that paid for if it is all to be revoted now, and what progress is being made?

The position is that a contract has been awarded to the B.C. Bridge and Dredge Company Limited and Northwestern Dredge Company Limited in the amount of $1,042,800. The date of completion for the dredging is set at August 7, 1955.
Has anything been paid yet for the work?
I am told now that the indication that the whole amount is a revote is in error, and that something has been paid for the work that has been done.

I wondered about that. It was also suggested that there should be a model of the whole harbour set up for the purpose of studying further changes in the first narrows. I should like to know whether or not that has been done and, if so, what progress has been made and when steps will be taken to do this additional work over and above the actual dredging of the first narrows which is now under way.
Supply-Public Works
I am told that the project is under the same committee which is studying Ripple rock and which reports through the national research council to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Can the minister tell us what progress has been made?
No, I cannot.

I find myself somewhat in the same position as I imagine a good many members do, that I am tempted to discuss some of the things that are not included in these estimates more than the ones which are. However, I do not propose to yield to that temptation except to draw to the attention of the minister another instance in which it would appear to me at least that it is a case of the left hand not knowing what the right hand is doing. I wish to refer to the West Coast Advocate, which is published in the city of Port Alberni. The issue of April 15 contains the following:
Also addressing the meeting-
Incidentally, the meeting was addressed by Mr. Arthur Laing, leader of the Liberal party in British Columbia.
-was . . . Irving Wilson, candidate in the 1953 federal contest. Mr. Wilson reviewed his recent trip to eastern Canada, and assured the meeting of the federal government's intentions on such local matters as the Alberni boat basin, west coast fishermen's floats . . .
The thing that struck me as being a bit strange was that at about the same time Mr. Wilson was solemnly assuring the people of the Alberni valley that the project on Kitsucksus creek, which is known as the Alberni boat basin, was going to be proceeded with. I received a letter which the minister may recall informed me that it had been decided not to proceed with that particular project. I thought the minister might be interested in knowing about that situation because it is a project in which the people of the city of Alberni particularly are quite interested.
Naturally they were rather disturbed at having been informed on the one hand by someone that the project was going to go ahead-at least, I understand so from the reports that were given to me-and on the other hand being regretfully informed by me, when I discussed the matter with the president and secretary of the board of trade, of the information I had from the minister. It did not create a particularly good situation.
However, there are one or two questions I should like to ask the minister about items that are included in this vote. The details are on page 468. There is one item, partly new and partly a revote, in connection with

Supply-Public Works
the project at French creek. The item reads, "Qualicum beach (French creek)-improvements". The people of that area are very much interested in that project. When I visited it while I was at home during the recess I was pleased to note that some considerable work had been done in the construction of the breakwaters since I had last seen it. However, as I understand the situation, the portion of the work which is included in this year's vote has not been completed and I would be very interested if the minister would give me details as to what further work is contemplated on that project.

In reply to my hon. friend's first statement about Alberni, the reason we have not been able to go ahead with the fishermen's floats is a dispute as to the adjoining property. That is the reason there was the change in contemplated action. I know my hon. friend will understand that things like that are bound to occur. The intention was to proceed, and had it not been for this dispute we would have done so.
At French creek, which is shown as Qualicum beach, the proposed improvements include enlarging the boat basin, extending the floats, constructing a diversion dam and rock breakwater. The construction of the breakwater is under contract with Ed Welsh and Company Limited at $32,130.

From the description the
minister has just given me, I take it that there is no provision for any deepening of the channel entrance leading into the basin itself. One of the reasons 1 asked that question is that I happened to see it for the first time at extreme low water on a recent visit.
There is no provision here for that, Mr. Chairman.

No provision for that? I should like to point out to the minister that before that project can be considered to be completed, in my opinion that is a necessary consideration. It does mean that a low water access to the basin is not available.
I shall certainly bear that in mind. I am glad to have these comments.

Item agreed to.
Harbours and rivers generally-
396.	Repairs and upkeep for the maintenance of services, including reconstruction and replacements, and to authorize commitments against future years in the total amount of $420,000, no new works to be undertaken, $3,535,000.

Will the minister explain this item, and in particular why it is necessary to have a vote of this size? In 1953-54 there was only $2,830,000 expended and in the

previous year $2,502,000 approximately, and yet we have a vote this year of $3,535,000.

As my hon. friend knows, this is the amount for repairs and upkeep of harbours and rivers generally, including reconstruction and replacement, but does not provide for any new work. Although it is estimated that the actual expenditure this year will be $2,830,000, the authorization under the vote included considerably more moneys than that. In fact, so far the funds for the last fiscal year authorized were $3,133,667.26. This is an estimate and the same remarks that I made earlier will apply here. If it is found we do not need this much money, we will certainly not carry it next year. It is one of those votes with respect to which I shall have to learn by experience.
Can the minister explain the purpose of this vote?
It is largely to provide for storm damage, which has been quite considerable in the fall of the year around my own part of the country, and I know that any seacoast is exposed to the same hazards.

Item agreed to.
Trans-Canada highway division-
397.	Administration, operation and maintenance, $487,484.
I understand that this item is for administration and covers the salaries of your own department for trans-Canada?
Yes, that is right.

Has the minister ever
thought of paying anything towards the maintenance of the highway after it is built? I know that is not contained in the agreement with the provinces, but something has to be done to encourage them to build more of these roads if we are going to complete the project in the seven-year period. Would the department consider something along that line?

My hon. friend knows I am limited by the provisions of the act. The act does not provide for maintenance but only for participation in the cost of construction, and I cannot go beyond that. I might add that when the provinces entered into the agreement to construct the highway by December 9, 1956, they did so knowing full well it provided only for the cost of construction and not for maintenance.

That was more or less a sort of horsetrading deal that was initiated. Probably you are a better horse trader than some of the provinces, so you got the best

of the deal. I think you have to do something to encourage the provinces to build more of this road or else take over the maintenance.

My friend is getting into a field that presents great difficulties. I am sure he knows there is still one province in Canada that has not signed the agreement because of stated fears of the invasion of a field of provincial jurisdiction. Maintenance of highways is a field that the provinces have always regarded as their own, and it would bring up a whole new series of problems which I believe are beyond the scope of anything that was contemplated when this act was being considered and finally approved.
Since the minister has mentioned that one province, is there any hope of getting that last province to sign the agreement within any reasonable time?
All I can say, Mr. Chairman, is that we are available.

In the details shown on page 470, there is an amount of $13,380 for film displays, broadcasting, advertising and other informational material other than publications; is that in connection with the trans-Canada highway and what purpose is served by that?

In the film board, we undertook some time ago to present a picture of Canada generally and at that time we used the vehicle of the royal visit, which was rather successful. I believe it was the most successful picture we ever made in the film board to interpret Canada to Canadians in a broad sense. We discussed another vehicle to try to develop that same sense of showing Canada as a whole to Canadians, and it occurred to us that the trans-Canada highway might be an appropriate means. We undertook, with the national film board, to share the costs of a film based upon the trans-Canada highway, but really designed for the purpose of showing Canada to Canadians in a manner that might appeal to them. That is the reason for that vote.
I see that item is down $10,000 this year. Does that mean you are not going to take another picture this year?
No, it is the same film.

There are two gaps that have not yet been constructed to a point where a vehicle can drive over them. One covers a distance of about 180 miles in Ontario and the other covers some 80 miles in Newfoundland. When these gaps will be closed is a matter for the provincial governments. We have been urging them, as I said before, but they have their own highway programs and their own highway problems. They are in the best position to judge how much of their total highway effort should be devoted to trans-Canada.
I said at that time the provinces did undertake by agreement to build their part of the highway by December 9, 1956. Now, it remains to be seen whether that is going to be achieved. We hope it will. I have written to all the provincial governments on several occasions-the last time was in December of last year-reminding them that the authority given to the government under the Trans-Canada Highway Act extends only to December 1956, and that we have no authority beyond that date.
Has the minister any idea of when these two gaps are to be closed?
No.
I suppose it will be some years earlier than completion of the system?

I cannot add to what I have said. The agreements provide for a termination date, and the provinces undertook to complete the highway by that date. I recognize the problems just as they do; but I do express the hope that they will be able to complete the highway on time. Some of the provinces will. The minister of highways of Alberta was in to see me this morning and indicated that he thought Alberta would finish on time. I believe Saskatchewan will, too; and there are others as well. Whether or not they all will is a matter for their own decision.
Will the minister be showing the gaps in the film of the trans-Canada highway?
Is there anything to come up in the near future by way of plans for a Yellowhead route?
The Yellowhead route is not part of the trans-Canada highway.
I believe it is designed as such.

But it is not designated as such, and that is the determining factor. The hon. member may have his own opinions

in the matter, but the fact of the matter is that the Yellowhead route has not been designated by the provinces concerned as the trans-Canada highway. That was their responsibility, and they chose another route.

And it was a very unhappy choice; I would like to say that. Would the government and the minister take kindly to considering the feasibility and possibility of building, as the most important part of the trans-Canada highway, the Yellowhead route, both from the point of view of economy and of service to the people. I would ask if, after the Big Bend highway is completed, the government would take kindly to building the Yellowhead route.

What is it my hon. friend wants?

It is easy to answer in the case of Quebec, because they have not started. With respect to Nova Scotia, to date two contracts have been awarded for bridges, but no work has been done on highway construction. I have here figures showing the number of miles approved and the number of miles completed. I shall have before me in a moment the total mileage in each province, and give the hon. member the information he wants.
In Newfoundland the total mileage of highways is 610 miles. There have been contracts of one kind or another approved for 236 miles, and the equivalent mileage completed is 139

miles. In Prince Edward Island the total mileage is 74; miles approved, 43-88; equivalent mileage completed 38-58. For Nova Scotia, as I said, contracts have been let for two bridges, and the total mileage to be completed is 310. Those two bridges are in Pictou county.
No work has been done on the highway.

No. Then, in New Brunswick the total mileage is 388; miles approved, 45-60; equivalent mileage completed 45-60. I wonder if we might call it six o'clock because I have several questions to ask.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. When the committee rose at six o'clock we were discussing item 397. Shall the item carry?

I would appreciate learning one or two things on this item, from the minister. I am sure that many hon. members, particularly those from British Columbia and Alberta, are concerned with certain problems that have arisen in connection with the construction of the trans-Canada highway in their portions of Canada. With respect to the Big Bend route of the trans-Canada highway, can the minister give us some clarification as to what in his opinion is the proper solution of the problem created by the proposed construction of the Mica creek dam, which, I understand, will affect the area for about 126 miles from

north to south and flood a portion of the highway construction? In view of the federal government's participation in the financing of the road, as well as the concern of the people of western Canada that there be no misconstruction, or waste of public funds, can the minister tell us whether any alternative route has been suggested? Surely the people of Canada would not want to see a highway built at the bottom of a lake.

Mr. Chairman, the route designated for the trans-Canada highway is along the Big Bend of the Columbia river. That is quite a long route. It is, I think, 195 miles from Revelstoke to Golden; whereas the direct distance is only about 95 miles, some 100 miles shorter. The problem is made more complicated by the location of a very good potential dam site at a place called Mica creek, at the north end of the Big Bend which, if built, would flood out a part of the route of the trans-Canada highway. We have been engaged with the government of British Columbia in trying to find an alternative route. Only last year we explored a pass called Rogers pass, which seems to have quite good possibilities. I am not at all sure the government of British Columbia shares our optimism as to the possibilities of building the road through the Rogers pass. In any event, the matter must soon be resolved one way or the other. We have also assured the government of British Columbia that if a trans-Canada highway were built around the route of the Big Bend and was subsequently flooded out they would be completely indemnified, as we would be, by the interests responsible for the building of the dam. In the meantime, this week, I had a discussion on that point with the minister of highways and public works of British Columbia, the Hon. Mr. Gaglardi, who told me it was his intention to start work this year on that part of the Big Bend which, under present planning, would be part of the trans-Canada but which, if that route were abandoned in favour of some other, would still be a necessary road, and the investment would not be lost as a result. The part of the road he has in mind is north from Revelstoke, and I understand it is his intention to start on it this year.

May I take this opportunity to ask another question of the minister? Has the government considered the advisability of building, in addition to the presently contemplated program of the trans-Canada highway, an additional trans-Canada highway from Winnipeg to Saskatoon, Edmonton, Edson and Jasper via the Yellowhead route to the west coast? In view of the unprecedented industrial development taking place in
Supply-Public Works
the central and northern part of Canada, it seems to me that such a road is very necessary. There is also the precarious position in which the north finds itself. From the standpoint of military necessity such a highway is also of primary importance. Further, has the government considered accepting the request of Premier Manning, acting on behalf of western provinces, which was made last spring, to discuss the matter of additional defence highways?
The discussion was held, Mr. Chairman, but the federal government took the view that the only commitment we have in mind at the present time relates to the building of the trans-Canada highway.

The minister mentioned Rogers pass. I believe that is the pass through which the Canadian Pacific Railway ran originally. When they built the long tunnel at Glacier they abandoned the road through Rogers pass. As I remember it, there was great trouble there with snow slides, and there were some very serious accidents on the railway as a result of those slides. Have the minister's engineers reported that as a favourable route for the highway?
The report we have is just based on a walking survey.
In the summertime?

Two of our engineers went through there. It is true it is a heavy snowfall area, and it is true that if the road should be built there would have to be considerable distances of snowsheds and other precautions; but even so, if it were feasible to build it through there the indications are that it would in any event be considerably cheaper than to build the extra 100 miles involved in the Big Bend highway, which in itself presents some very difficult construction problems.

Could the minister have a check made of the route from Golden south and then through the mountains to the head of Kootenay lake and from there up to Arrowhead and Revelstoke? Some suggestion has been made that that would be an easier way to get across the Selkirk mountains. It might be worth while to have that route checked.

The position is of course that the designation of the route is the responsibility of the provincial government; but we would certainly be happy to examine with them any possible route through the mountains between Revelstoke and Golden.

I presume that the major portion of the $2 million which is to be voted for this year's expenditure will be on the trans-Canada highway through Banff park, with the remainder on the adjoining park in British Columbia. When is it intended to complete the trans-Canada highway, of which practically none is completed through Banff national park?

As my hon. friend knows, we have been doing a considerable amount of work from the east gate into the town of Banff and into Lake Louise. Just when we shall complete that portion of the work in Banff park, I am not prepared to say; but we intend to push on with the construction of the road in both parks, which is our sole responsibility.

-runs out with the provinces for the completion of the trans-Canada highway?

I would hope we would be able to do that. It will be a big task because construction there is difficult. There are still long distances to be built. Subject to our being able to have funds voted by parliament and to overcome physical difficulties in the way of doing it, we hope to be able to complete it on time. On page 470 where details are given of item 398, we find an item of $24,300 required for increases in rates of pay. May I ask the minister for an explanation of that item? The reason why I ask for it is
[Mr. Winters.!

this. Last year there was no provision for the increase. Did these people not get an increase when the rest of the civil servants received one last year?
These people are not civil servants.
Did they not get an increase last year? There is no provision made for them.
I am told that this is a matter of the form of bookkeeping; that there was an increase last year but that it is incorporated in the other figures.

The reason why I asked the question was this. This increased pay is for the number of 86 employees spread over a year. If they did receive an increase last year, it was not very much. It means only about $5 a week. If they were not treated favourably last year, I do not think they have had enough.
There was a general increase last year and again this year.

399.	To provide for remedial works where damages are caused by. or endanger, navigation or federal government structures and to complete protection works already under way, $500,000.
Will the minister explain this item and give us examples of what projects this money is used for?

This money is spent largely on rivers where there is river bank erosion resulting from navigation or which is likely to endanger navigation or which is attributable to some government structure, such as some breakwater or wharf which sets up the kind of currents which contribute towards erosion. There are many examples along the St. Lawrence river where there is erosion resulting from the passage of ships and the wakes they throw up. We have spent a considerable amount of money on them. One good example is that at Longueuil on the south side of the St. Lawrence river east of St. Lambert, I think it is, across from Montreal. A considerable amount of money has been spent there. 401.	To provide for advance planning of projects Including acquisition of sites, $500,000.

I should like to ask a question or two on this item. It apparently is to provide for advance planning of projects including acquisition of sites, $500,000. This afternoon the chairman ruled that we could

not ask about unemployment. However, I presume it will be quite in order to talk about those who are on an enforced holiday without remuneration. I want to ask the minister this question. Is this item in the estimates with a view to the planning of projects that can utilize the services of persons who are unemployed in the future? Is that the particular purpose of this item?
No. It is not the primary purpose of the item.

What projects are being
considered? What I mean is this. Is the planning itself to cost $500,000? It must be quite extensive.

No. It is not really very extensive at all. As a matter of fact, it is a very small vote for the purpose. As I have indicated previously, we hope that in the future we shall be able to bring items to a sufficient stage of planning that, when we carry an amount in the estimates, we shall be able to get on with the work. Heretofore, in some instances votes have been put in the estimates before sites were acquired and before planning was undertaken. The result was that they had to be voted year after year and I think a good many members became tired of seeing revotes in the estimates with no construction taking place. This is a means for doing something about that matter. We propose to do some planning so that when we put an item in the estimates we shall be able to get on with the work. That is the intention behind it.
We are all for that procedure.
This vote is to be used for two purposes, apparently?
Yes.
One is for planning?
Yes.
For preparing plans?
Yes.
And the other is for acquiring sites?
That is correct.

How is the amount to be
divided between those two objectives?

There is no attempt here to divide it between them. It is just to be used as required for the acquisition of sites and for some planning. We have not endeavoured to break it down. It is just

a lump sum being carried for the first time. Here again we shall have to gain experience with it.
Is it intended that the sum will be $500,000 each year?
I could not say that.
Or are there likely to be big increases?

I will say this. It will be varied as conditions require, either upward pr downward; I do not know which it will be. This is just a rough guess, a method to try to make for a little bit more orderly presentation of the estimates.

Possibly it would be appropriate for me to express at this time the hope that part of this $500,000 may be used to acquire sites and to make plans for those five projects which I brought to the attention of the minister prior to this time, namely the five projects which were approved by parliament last May. I trust that the minister will not overlook the crying necessity for progress with respect to those projects. We trust that we shall learn soon that at least the sites have been acquired for those five projects, including the one in my own home town, and that the preparation of plans is going forward without delay. I have just returned from my home town and I may say to the minister that that is the hope expressed by all of the citizens of that community.

Why is it necessary to have this item in the estimates in view of the changes being made in the administration ot the department? 405.	Emergency shelter administration (formerly under department of resources and development), $25,000.

Mr. Chairman, I believe this item is the first of three relating to housing, the others being items 406 and 535. I do not propose this evening, Mr. Chairman, to precipitate any general discussion on housing. There have been some sessions since the war when there have been altogether too few opportunities for the discussion of housing policy in general. But this session is not of that nature. I suppose housing has had more ample discussion at this session than in any session during the post-war period. We had an extended discussion of the new National Housing Act on second reading; we had it before the banking and commerce committee for some weeks, where it was submitted to what I believe may be called very intensive study; we had a further discussion at some length in committee of the whole when the bill was reported back to the house for third reading. For that reason, Mr. Chairman, I believe there is no occasion now for any extended debate on housing policy in general.
However, Mr. Chairman, I have a question in regard to this item in particular, which covers an amount of $25,000 for emergency shelter administration. This has been a dwindling item for some years. The amount appropriated last year, I see, was $35,000, but if we have regard to the details on page 473 we will find that in the previous fiscal year expenditure reached a total of $454, and that in the fiscal year just closed there had not been any money spent at all up to December 31. The estimate of the amount required for the remaining three months of the fiscal year was also nil Therefore I am led to ask why there should be anything in the estimates under this item this year. What need can now remain?

The need remains, Mr. Chairman, to keep these properties we still have in good shape and fit as living accommodation. This is not an item on which the taxpayers are required to carry any burden. The operation carries itself, but it is necessary to come to parliament to get a vote each year for the necessary expenditures on capital additions or changes to the accommodation. That is something one cannot predict accurately. We thought $25,000 little enough, but whether that will be spent I do not know. If it requires to be spent in order to keep the accommodation in shape then we shall have to have it.

Mr. Chairman, I believe we are all aware of the relationship of which the minister speaks between appropriations under this item and net cost to the public
Supply-Public Works
treasury, but he will have to make out a better case for an appropriation under this item than he has yet made out. Will he tell us exactly how much was spent on this item in the fiscal year ended March 31?

We spent no money this year on them, but under the terms of agreement for these projects Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has a contingent liability to restore the sites in the event that the projects are vacated. They have been gradually abandoning these areas and in those cases it has been necessary to restore the sites. It is entirely possible there may be some site restoration this year, and in that event this money will be required.

I do not think that is a very satisfactory or convincing case. Not a cent of money was required last year, not a copper! There was $35,000 appropriated by parliament for the purpose indicated by the minister and not one cent was required. Now we are asked to provide $25,000 for a purpose which did not require a cent of expenditure last year. Surely the minister is not seriously going to ask the house to appropriate $25,000 when not a copper was required. This is an item that has been dwindling year by year. The need has shrunk rather than increased, and I suggest there is no reason to expect that anything more is going to be required during this new fiscal year than was actually required during the fiscal year just closed. I suggest to the minister that if he is thinking of some unforeseeable needs he would be well provided if he had $5,000 in his estimates for that purpose. I suggest that to him seriously.

I am pleased to have that serious suggestion, but we have projects at Edmonton, Regina, Brantford, Saint John, Sydney, Halifax and Long Branch, and I do not think it would be entirely prudent, with all these tenants, to assume, for example, that just because a water main did not break last year one will not break this year. I am very glad to have the serious suggestion of the hon. member for Eglinton, but I would not want to take the responsibility of having something happen this year that we could not cope with for lack of this amount of money which I am sure my hon. friend will agree is quite a modest sum in relation to the projects we have to handle.
I was just about to ask the minister where these emergency shelters were located, but he has answered that. How many people are now housed in emergency shelters across Canada?
Approximately 1,000 people.

Would the department take that into consideration, in a project of this nature involving 1,200 families? That would mean a large influx in a brand new area. Who accepts responsibility for community centres?

The experience in Central Mortgage in connection with war workers houses by way of providing community centres has not always been the kind of experience that would lead them to go into a community centre on this project.
I know my hon. friend could make out a good case for it. But the fact of the matter

Perhaps this matter should have been attended to when the land was being bought and laid out for a residential area. I do not know whether the minister has seen the project-

-but, when it started, part of it was in my constituency. I remember there were a number of headaches getting things straightened out; but I believe finally they were straightened out. Some attempt should be made to assist these people in acquiring land nearby, if it is available, for community centres. We have gone into that sort of thing in Vancouver in most residential areas. This is a large and compact one and, as it is new, the quality of the residences is fairly good. But more than that, the population consists almost entirely of young married couples with families. To have no community centre for recreation is a condition that should be remedied now, if it can be.

I imagine I might as well speak out plainly now, instead of approaching the matter indirectly. So I shall ask my question in a direct fashion: Let me point out, first, that this project is in part of my old provincial riding. I was interested in one remark the minister made when he pointed out that an average of $1,000 per unit is being asked for 344 housing units. Where are they located and how long ago were they constructed? How does it happen that these extensive repairs are required, averaging $1,000 per unit?

These are old wartime war workers houses. They had no basements or foundations, and this is an attempt to improve them by putting permanent foundations under them. I am sure my hon. friend has seen this going on all across the country. It is a quite expensive undertaking, but it does improve the houses substantially. It requires new foundations and often new sills. Quite often dry rot has set in. It is the old vintage of wartime housing.
Then it is a great deal more than repairs?
I said it amounted to permanent improvements to war workers houses.
I was referring to the minister's last remark when he mentioned 344 units at $1,000 each, and I understood used the word "repair".
If I used that word, I used it incorrectly, but I do not recall that I used it.
I understand then that it is really the reconstruction of units that were constructed without cellars.

I ask as to the kind of contracts under which new units are being constructed at Gander and elsewhere. What type of contract is being used by Central Mortgage?
They are all firm bid contracts.

Yes.

It depends on the vintage of the houses and the degree of repairs they need when foundations are put under them. I am told that at one time Central Mortgage and Housing made such allowance up to $700, but the amount indicated is an estimate of likely present-day costs.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
On this opening item of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources there is a matter that I should like to call to the attention of the minister. It has to do with the subject of an island in lake Erie, Ontario. This island is a very interesting place indeed from many points of view. It is approximately 14 miles long and varies in width from approximately 1 mile to 3 miles and averages approximately 14 miles in width. There are more than 17,000 acres of land on this island. It juts out from the Canadian shore of lake Erie and stretches out toward the middle of lake Erie almost to the international boundary line. The start of the island, which, owing to the filling in of the marshes, makes it in reality a sort of peninsula rather than an island, forms a long bay about 18 miles wide at the mouth and diminishes to only a few hundred yards in width at the narrow end. This particular island to which I refer would probably make a wonderful site for a national park for various reasons, which are as follows:
First of all, this large island is located within 150 miles of probably the most thickly populated part of the Dominion of Canada. It is in southwestern Ontario and is part of the county of Norfolk. If this island were made a national park it would then be available as a playground and a place which could be visited not only by our own people there but by tourists from the United States as well, and we all know that tourist trade from the United States is very valuable indeed. In addition, this island is a veritable paradise for wildlife. I understand there are more snakes on the island per square foot than anywhere else in the world, but none of the snakes are poisonous. There is one particular variety there which I believe is found nowhere else in North America. It is called the "wamper", a large water snake, from six to eight feet long. It is harmless, although it might cause nervous shock or something of that kind if arrived upon unexpectedly.
There are also eagles on this island, and in the waters adjoining the island there is probably the best small-mouth bass fishing in North America. There may be other places which are as good. I say that in deference to other hon. members, but I do not think that any other place is better. In addition to that, this particular island is also one of the very finest duck-shooting places in North America. The reason for that is the large bay that is formed by this island and the mainland of Ontario and the rest of lake Erie. Because of the fact that this island is nothing more or less than a gigantic sandbar, there are a lot of shallow inlets and bays and small islands

adjoining the inshore side of this long island or small peninsula. In these little bays the waters are not more than a few inches to a few feet deep, and there are large quantities of wild rice which attract a great many game birds in the fall, wild ducks, geese and so on. The island also has a very large stand of virgin timber, which is a rarity in that part of Canada. And, particularly, some of the hardwoods grow to a great size, which is also unique. Unfortunately the present owners of the island are cutting down this timber and selling it.
Hon. members may very well ask why these things exist, and I shall come to that in a moment. The island also has great historic value. It stretches right out in lake Erie and has often been called the Sable island of the great lakes. More ships have been wrecked around this island than anywhere else in all the great lakes put together. As I have already pointed out, the whole island for that matter is a shifting sandbar. Right off the end of the island is a very deep hole, I believe the deepest spot in lake Erie, which, compared with the other lakes, is not very deep, not more than 200 feet deep. The end of the island has been shifting with the winds and currents and as a result during the last century and indeed in this century there have been a great many wrecks.
For those who were able to land on the island without being chased off by the gamekeeper it has often been a source of great interest to see the wreckage of some of these old ships poking up through the sand. Many books have been written about this place. Possibly a number of hon. members have read some of them. It is also of interest that in the war of 1812 when General Brock set out from Port Dover in some small boats, to capture Detroit-which he did quite successfully-the party rowed around this island, landed at one point on it and camped there all night.
There are many other points of interest. At the present time the eastern tip of the island is still retained, I believe, by the federal government and a large lighthouse station is maintained there, whose light guides vessels safely through lake Erie and away from the highly dangerous end of this island. For those who are unfamiliar with this particular piece of land may I say this. When there is still all this wildlife on this island and it is still in the virgin state, there may be many who are wondering why people are not allowed to go on it. The reason is extremely interesting indeed. In the year 1866, which even for Ontario is a relatively
Supply-Northern Affairs long while ago-I would remind hon. members it was before confederation-a special act of incorporation was passed by the legislature of Upper Canada. This act incorporated a company called the Long Point Company. The original directors were to be John Brown, George Hamilton Gillespie, Thomas Cockburn Kerr, William Little, David Tisdale, Lauchlin McCallum and Samuel DeVoe Woodruff. It is rather interesting to note that these gentlemen I have just mentioned were all Canadians and that they all came from different parts of what is now the province of Ontario. One came from Hamilton, one came from St. Catharines, another from London, another from Simcoe and so on. It is also interesting to note that two months before this act of incorporation was passed, these same gentlemen had purchased from the crown virtually all the lands which make up this island of Long Point. Some small parts of those lands were acquired later by the company, but most of the lands were acquired by these same gentlemen from the crown at that time. Hon. members may be able to draw their own conclusions-that is the only thing they can do since all these people are, of course, long dead and gone-as to why they came from different parts of Ontario when they acquired these lands from the crown. In due course these same gentlemen, being the directors at the time of the incorporation of the company, sold this whole island to the company.
It is interesting to note what the objects and purposes of this company were. Paragraph 3 of the act of incorporation reads as follows:
The company may carry on the business of pursuing, protecting and granting licences to take game, muskrats, mink, otter, beaver, and fish, upon the said lands and property or in the water covering the same: and generally the doing of such other acts or things with the said land or with any mineral substance or thing, grown, or to be grown, found or being in or upon the same, as may promote the interests of the company,-
Then they very nicely put in this qualification:
-and not being contrary to the laws of this province, or the terms of the patent from the crown.
Then one of the most interesting items of all is paragraph 4 of this act of incorporation which reads as follows:
The capital stock of the company shall be the sum of fifty thousand dollars, divided into one hundred shares of five hundred dollars each, . . .
Then it goes on to say that this amount may be increased from time to time. It is interesting to notice that the purchase price paid for all this land by the new company to these

Supply-Northern Affairs same gentlemen who had originally purchased it from the crown was one hundred shares of the company. For those of you who are familiar with the rudiments of corporation law, the implication is obvious. For those who are not, let me say this. The fact remains that while the shares in the company were to be one hundred shares of five hundred dollars each, the land given in exchange for these shares was fully paid up. In other words, the land was virtually turned over in exchange for these shares. On the face of it there seems to be nothing particularly wrong with any of this procedure. But let us go into the history of this company and this island a little bit further.
It has been a well-known fact-and to everyone in that part of the country it is common knowledge-that the in fact owners of the company have ever since that date been a number of extremely wealthy men from New York city and the surrounding areas. Occasionally there has been a Canadian member. At the present time I believe there are two and possibly three Canadian members of this club. The rest of them are all citizens of the United States. The late J. P. Morgan, of considerable financial fame, was one of the owners, or was one of the members and shareholders of this company. Many other men with prominent names in American business and financial history have been owners and members of this club. I do not wish to take up the time of the committee to go into this matter at any great length, but the information is easily available.
As I understand it this club-and I say this in order to be fair-has kept up the objects and purposes that were set out in the original charter. They have been scrupulously careful about the taking of game. It is my understanding that the members of this club go to the club only during the duck-shooting season in the fall and that they take only a few ducks, something which is extremely admirable indeed. I understand that they seldom if ever attended the place during the bass-fishing season. I may say that there have been some extremely noted visitors to the club. His Majesty King Edward VIII, while Prince of Wales, was a guest at the club, and I understand he did some shooting there at the time of his visit. Of course that was quite a number of years ago.
To get back to the original suggestion, I feel that this island should become a national park and the property of all the people of Canada, not only for the use of our citizens but as a wonderful attraction for tourists as well. It is quite true that the Long Point Company and its shooting and game club have done a very good job of preserving the wildlife there; and I think they should be


commended for what they have done. While it is true that it may not have been all a matter of altruism, because by keeping everybody else off the island they actually protected the game and fish there for themselves, the fact remains that, no matter what was their reason for doing it, this is a wonderful preserve of wildlife and it is one of the few places of its kind anywhere in the settled or populated parts of Canada.
In addition to the Long Point club itself there is one other club known as the Rice Bay club which is situate in the water area near the shore. This club is set up on stilts on the water and is not actually attached to the land. I understand that they always manage to get along very well with the Long Point Company and the residents of this club have never been asked to leave. I would think it would be quite possible, if these lands were obtained for the public benefit, that there would be no necessity to disturb the people who have had possession and who have enjoyed certain rights there but that they could be left alone. However, I am quite sure that the members of the Long Point Company do not need an island nearly fourteen miles long and a mile and a half wide purely for their own purposes. There should be a good road through the island so that the public can come in, as they do in other natural parks, and see nature as it is under unique circumstances.
There is one other thing of interest about this island and that is what I may call the bay side, which is very swampy and full of wildlife such as snakes and so on, and which would be ideal for setting up any type of reserve. The southern or lakeside shore of the island has one of the most beautiful natural beaches in Canada with very fine, hard, white sand stretching for miles and would be suitable for holidayers. Now the far end of the island, that is the end closest to the mainland, which was never acquired by this company, is at the present time leased by the province of Ontario to cottagers on a 99-year lease basis with certain restrictions on the type of cottages that can be put up there. There are many hundreds of cottages, though in fact only a few have the advantage of a lakefront site. Most of them are in plots of sand toward the middle of the island. These cottagers come largely from places such as London, Woodstock, Tillsonburg, Brantford, Simcoe, Toronto, Hamilton and many other places, as well as from the United States. I know that a great many people from my own riding have summer cottages there and a great many people also have small cabins which they use on fishing and shooting expeditions. At the opening of the bass season

anywhere within three miles of this particular island there are not dozens but hundreds of boats out fishing. For those who have been there it is indeed a unique spot. I could go on, Mr. Chairman, but I do not think it is necessary to discuss this matter at any further length. I think the main idea has been put across to the minister.
However, I understand that there are other islands and areas in Ontario which could be turned into national parks. The minister was kind enough to give me this information, since I did not have time to look it up myself, but I understand that one of these areas is Pelee island, which is at the opposite end of lake Erie near the city of Windsor. I think it would be a rather suitable thing if some arrangement could be made with the Ontario government so that this island, Long Point, can also be acquired as a national park, as well as Pelee island.
I would like to wind up these remarks by emphasizing that such natural assets showing Canadian wildlife as it is in that part of Ontario, and which have remained unspoiled, should become the property of everyone in Canada and should not remain the property of a few very wealthy people from the United States.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I simply wish to say a word as to the policy of the government as regards the setting up of national parks. As hon. members are aware, the first prerequisite is that the land for a park be offered by a provincial government to us free of all encumbrances, and it is only after such an offer has been made that the various factors which have to be taken into account before we can come to a decision are in fact considered.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few brief observations on the first item in these estimates, but before proceeding to do so I must say that I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech of the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. His speech was most interesting and informative.
This is a department which during recent years has frequently changed its name and certain branches have been rearranged from time to time. It is, in my opinion, a very important department indeed and one of those departments which offer tremendous opportunity and scope for a minister with talent and imagination, and also a great opportunity for action in regard to the natural resources of this country. I might say, Mr. Chairman, that we are indeed fortunate in having a young minister in charge of this department face to face with some very
Supply-Northern Affairs ancient problems. I hope the combination of the two will distil a very satisfactory result.
I have read the entire report issued by this department because it always makes interesting reading. I think the officials who compiled this report are to be congratulated on issuing a most interesting document. I am, of course, referring to the report tabled on March 31, 1953, while it was still the department of resources and development. I found the report interesting, comprehensive and excellent in every way.
I wish to make again the suggestion I have made on previous occasions when dealing with these estimates, that in my opinion the estimates of this department should be referred to the committee on mines, forests and waters. That committee has not met for quite a number of years and this is a committee that could do a good deal of useful work. I am not suggesting that the estimates should be submitted solely for examination, to ascertain how the money should be spent. I think the estimates should be submitted to the committee so that the committee will have an opportunity to hear from various excellent technical personnel in this department in regard to the amount of work they are doing. There are quite a number of men in this department doing very useful work of which very few Canadians, and indeed I believe a small percentage of the members of this house, are aware, and I think the referring of these estimates to that committee would be well worth while and provide members of this house with an opportunity to learn about the work being done by this very important department.
That is all I am going to say about the estimates at this time. But I do want to say a few words-I see the minister looking at me and I am quite sure he knows what I am about to say-in regard to the recent resources conference held in Ottawa, the first I might say since 1906. This conference was sponsored by the Canadian Forestry Association, the Agricultural Institute of Canada, the Canadian Forestry Institute, the Canadian Institute of Engineers and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. I am sure the minister will agree that it was an excellent conference, at which I spent a most enjoyable two days. I must say I listened with a great deal of interest to the minister's welcoming speech. It was a very interesting speech and indeed a capable speech which was received very favourably by the delegates present. I hope that as a result of the work of the conference and their findings the minister when he next addresses an
4270	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs organization of that type, or even in addressing this house, will commit the government to some definite action along the lines suggested by the conference.
Two days were spent dealing with the important question of renewable natural resources. There was an excellent discussion on our forest resources and another on soil and water resources, and yet another on wildlife and recreational facilities. Papers were read and discussions were held by people who knew what they were talking about, and some of the most prominent people in Canada working in these spheres made some excellent speeches which were well worth listening to, while the discussion on their papers was interesting indeed.
As the result of these two days of papers, addresses and discussions, the conference summarized its opinions. It did not pass a formal resolution but more or less by general agreement summarized the findings of the conference. I think it is quite fair to say that the opinion was generally expressed that there should be a national policy in the development of our natural resources devised as the result of dominion-provincial cooperation. That question was mentioned again and again in the papers and discussions that followed.
It was also suggested by several speakers that a royal commission should be established to study the whole question of conservation of natural resources in Canada, to gather evidence, hear opinions, and make recommendations and prepare a report. I was also very interested to notice that repeatedly, whether the speaker came from British Columbia, the prairies, central Canada or the maritimes, the opinion was expressed that we must have a national approach to this problem and that there should be greater contributions from the federal government towards a general overall national conservation policy in Canada.
These were not the opinions of people who had not given consideration to the subject. These were the opinions of people who have lived with these various questions, forest resources, soil and water conservation, wildlife and recreational problems, for many years, and that was a summary of their opinions. I hope that as the result of that conference and its findings, as the result of the meeting together of minds of people prominent in these fields from the Atlantic to the Pacific, the government will give some consideration to the findings of the conference. I trust that the immediate result will be an increase in the estimates of this department next year in order to assist the provinces with respect to forest protection,
[Mr. Herridge.l

soil and water conservation, conservation of wildlife and recreational resources.
I do not know whether the minister has received any formal representations from the conference but I would certainly like the minister to give consideration to the opinions expressed there and to inform the house if the government is being moved in the direction of calling a dominion-provincial conference to establish a national policy on conservation as the result of consultation and co-operation.
