maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have received a letter from my good friend, Mr. Van Camp, but I have not yet received the resolutions adopted at that conference. My hon. friend may rest assured that the officers of my department and I will give these resolutions all the consideration that they certainly deserve.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Assuming that we will not conclude consideration of the national parks branch tonight, possibly what I am about to say might be taken as notice by the minister because I am sure that he and his officials will want the opportunity to secure the information which I require. The minister may or may not recall that last December, when we were considering amendments respecting the operation and maintenance of parks, I asked a question to this effect. I wanted to know what rights go with leases when leases are granted in park areas or in areas under the jurisdiction of the parks branch. After I had said that I had certain information with respect to a bad situation in connection with Banff national park, the minister asked me to submit the information to him. I thanked him and said I would, but I must say that it has taken me until this time to get all the information I wanted.
Last week I was asked to meet two different organizations for the purpose of discussing this matter. The area I have in mind is just outside Banff national park and is known as the Ya-Ha-Tinda area. It covers eighteen square miles and consists of portions of township 32, ranges 11 and 12, west of the fifth meridian. According to an order in council passed on the 14th of March, 1950, which I have before me, this area was set apart for the use of the dominion parks branch for grazing purposes. I have heard that a ranch is now established in that area.
But, Mr. Chairman, these are the complaints. Is this still a park area? It is under the jurisdiction of the parks branch, but is it still a park area? If so, do the rules and regulations governing parks apply here? This is what we find. In this area of eighteen square miles some persons are permitted to hunt big game and some are denied the right. Rangers have stopped certain persons

from going in there but when these hunters have challenged the jurisdiction of the ranger no action has been taken.
On the gate leading into the property is a no trespassing sign. Apparently the no trespassing sign applies to some people but does not apply to others because certain persons have been refused entry to this eighteen square mile area while others have been permitted to enter. I do not mind telling the minister that the meetings I had last week were with two branches of the fish and game association. These hunters have gone in there and have seen hunting going on. They have seen game shot and taken out of the area and yet they themselves have been excluded from this eighteen square mile area and have been threatened with prosecution if they enter.
These people say to me that if this area is to be a game preserve, as are the park sections, that is fine, they have no complaint; but if it is to be an area in which some people are allowed to hunt, then all should be allowed to hunt there. They tell me that recently a part of the area has been plowed up and they think that is strange. They say it is a mistake. Part of the area is very similar to the prairies and has a type of grass known as prairie wool. If that is removed it will be an absolute disaster.
In this eighteen square mile area there is some of the finest scenery that you would want to see, and yet according to the sign on the gate and according to the orders given by the rangers it is closed entirely to the public. They think there is something strange about all this. This has been the experience for a number of years now and these men would like to get true information with respect to the situation. If the area is closed, if the public are completely excluded, they want to know it. If those in authority have the right to put up a no trespassing sign on the gate then these people would like to know it. A very good road leads right up to the gate where the no trespassing sign is posted. Cars can move right up to that point. Within a matter of three miles inside a most beautiful waterfall can be seen. Yet, as I say, these people are ordered out of there and are warned what will happen if they go in. On the other hand, others go in there and camp. I was asked if I would look into the matter. I may say that I have just returned today and I had hoped to be able to get the facts together a little better. I trust that this matter can be straightened out so that I can advise these people as to the true situation that exists in that eighteen square mile area.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I ask one question for clarification? Would the hon. member say who has been doing the warning he is talking about?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The rangers.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The park employees?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes; they must be park rangers because these men told me it was a federal park ranger. Under the order in council, Mr. Chairman, it says:
Whereas the Minister of the Interior reports that it is proposed to withdraw certain lands including Ya-Ha-Tinda area from the Rocky Mountains park, Alberta, and that the said area is now used and will continue to be required by the dominion parks branch for winter grazing:
Therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in Council . . .
As you will note, it was set aside out of the region by the parks branch, presumably for winter grazing. Then down below it states:
. . . also withdrawn from disposal under the said act and set apart for the use of the dominion parks branch for grazing purposes.
These men tell me it is a federal forest ranger who is in there and who orders them off the place. Incidentally, he misses an island, apart from the park proper, but there is provincial land all around him. Here is the order in council. I have seen recent correspondence between certain of these men who have complained to the provincial government. The provincial government has had some correspondence with the federal authority in connection with it. I believe the province recommended that a corridor be cleared into this area in the park. In any event, quite a number of these letters are filed, and it is most disturbing and most confusing. Perhaps the minister would like to look into it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member if he would hand me a copy of the order in council that he had in his hand? That would help me clarify the position. Perhaps then I will be able to answer his question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes. I assumed the minister would want some time to look into this subject and that was my reason for bringing it up now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
There are two small items I might perhaps mention here. The first one Is the site of Batoche, about which the minister or his assistants are probably well informed. There is a need there for a building of some sort which is a permanent site. I will not go into the history. I understand there is an old building there now which has been offered to the department and I understand from the departmental officials that the price being asked for that building is perhaps too high. I would be inclined perhaps to agree with that. I would urge, though, that this department might consider proceeding with that piece of business. I know there have been negotiations, but I feel the amount the department has offered for this particular building might be considered too low. I just wanted to draw that to the minister's attention, in the hope that perhaps negotiations would be continued so that that permanent place, which has a great connection with Saskatchewan's history, might be preserved.
There is a road there, too, but I do not know whether it will come entirely under the provincial government or whether the dominion department would consider it had some responsibility. It is a historic road up


which certain troops went at the time of the rebellion. It runs along the river bank, and although I do not quite know where it is, it is in the same Batoche district near the historic battleground. I do know the people there would like to get the matter settled so there would be some permanency about it.
The other item, I suggest, might come more nearly under the heading of museums. We of course, in the province of Saskatchewan, unfortunately have not very much history. I feel we should make an effort to preserve what history there is. I should like to pay tribute to a man who has devoted the important part of his life to the preservation of things historical in that province. He is Campbell Innis, who was formerly a school inspector and I think has acted for the department in an official capacity in connection with the historic site of the old town of Battleford. At the town of Battleford there is the old mounted police barracks and a very interesting and well kept museum on the site of the old fort.
After that had been established, and after the dominion government had taken some interest in it, a few various old implements of one sort or another began to be gathered together. Saskatchewan, of course, has been an agricultural province. The things to which I am referring are things like the buffalo carts, the Red river carts, as they called them, and the first machinery that was used in the breaking up of that country for agriculture. A collection finally developed and was gathered together in one or two places in the northern part of the province, I think somewhere around North Battleford or Battleford, and some in my own city of Saskatoon. I would hope that the minister would come out to Saskatoon-and I give him a hearty invitation to do so. As I said the other day, during two weeks of the election campaign we had five cabinet ministers out there. I do not think the minister now before the committee was one of them; but he would foe welcomed if he did come. As I said the other day, I am here to return the visit of those cabinet ministers.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: He was not a minister then. Perhaps he will come next time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: At any rate, to go back to my story: the point I wish to make is that we have a marvellous collection out there-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I will come to see it in a month and a half.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
-of instruments of transportation used in the early days, beginning with the Red river cart. Then we go into agricultural implements, and we have ancient buggies, and all sorts of things. We have had

a grant from the provincial government- and I have no doubt the minister will tell me that this is provincial rather than federal business, because cabinet ministers in the dominion departments of government have a habit of saying that.
At any rate, after these things had sat out in the elements for a long time, finally some well-intentioned people got them housed under one roof. They brought them down to my city. On the west side of that city there is a place something in the shape of a hangar in which all these old implements have been gathered. A crew of men was hired. The old building was scraped out and renovated, and put into shape for exhibition. The place is now full of those relics.
The Minister of Agriculture was out in Saskatchewan during the Easter recess, and I believe he was invited to look over these things. However, he was not able to come, because he was on other forms of business. If he had gone he would have been interested to see the buggy that was driven over the Saskatchewan plains for a good many years by his predecessor, the late Hon. W. R. Motherwell, whose name, as a former minister of agriculture, is treated with great respect both in the House of Commons and in the country.
I suggest that the department of the minister to whom I am addressing these remarks might take some interest in the matter, and accept some responsibility for the exhibition of these objects. I do know that the provincial government has given a fair grant, and that the municipality of Saskatoon has done something for them. Finally they got these things in out of the weather, and necessary repairs have been done. I have no doubt thousands of tourists will look over the exhibition this year. While I am not sure, I think a small admission fee is charged. If it is, the revenue will be used for maintenance.
I know, however, that at the moment a cement floor is required in that museum. That would put the finishing touches on it. I am merely suggesting that when the new minister looks over his historic sites, museums, and that sort of thing, he might look at this one. I know that the national museum comes under his department and I see no reason why, if a national library should have branches throughout the country-and I am happy that it has-a national museum should not be treated in the same way. Those of us from Saskatchewan are in favour of that sort of thing. I believe it is important that we preserve our connection with the past.
That is all I wish to say on the matter. I simply draw it to the minister's attention
Supply-Northern Affairs in the hope that he will look into it and give some consideration as to whether or not he would be justified in seeing that this institution receives some support from this department of the federal government.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As to the first point raised by the hon. member, I am quite familiar with the question of the old rectory at Batoche. That this is an historic site of great historic value, I would be the first to agree. But of course we cannot buy historic value, because it is impossible to appraise or to evaluate it in money terms. We have to purchase at the appraised value any building or lands we may require. In this instance the price asked was $10,000, while the appraisal made was around $1,500.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think the offer of the dominion government also was $1,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
No, the offer was not $1,500. We said $10,000 was not a reasonable price, and we asked if they would not bring the price down to a reasonable figure-because certainly I was ready to recommend a figure higher than the $1,500, if we could come to a settlement. However, the owners have not seen fit to come down a single cent from the $10,000.
Again, I am very much aware of the historic value of that site, because it is part of the Riel history, which I have known for years. I shall be meeting with members of the historic sites and monuments board on June 7 and 8, when they have their annual meeting here in Ottawa, and I am going to discuss with them some other solution to the problem with a view to satisfying the owners and at the same time maintaining the policy in the department, which we believe is sound and should be followed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in contrast with what was said by the hon. member for Saskatoon, in British Columbia we are very rich in history. On that account I have always been interested in marking historic sites and monuments. For some years I urged that a monument be erected to David Thompson at the Castlegar-Robson crossing of the Columbia. I was informed about a year ago that the board had agreed to the suggestion, and that a monument was going to be erected at a suitable place. What is the reason for the delay? I do not think anything has happened to date.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
There is a general reason, that we are late in setting up these plaques that have been recommended by the historic sites and monuments board. We have a definite budget, and we try to do as much as we can each year. However, to date, we have

Supply
not been able to keep pace with the recommendations of the board. That is the general answer to the hon. member's question. However, I shall look into the matter in particular and see that there is not too much delay in the case he has mentioned.
